title: Ziina Launches Split Bill to Simplify Shared Group Payments
snippet: UAE fintech Ziina launches Split Bill, letting users divide group expenses, automate payment reminders, and track settlements as annual volume tops $2 billion. The post Ziina Launches Split Bill to Simplify Shared Group Payments appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Homegrown UAE financial platform Ziina has launched Split Bill, a new feature extending its consumer peer-to-peer (P2P) offering to streamline how users request, track, and settle shared group expenses. The rollout comes as the Dubai-headquartered fintech crosses major operational milestones, reaching over one million annual users and surpassing US$2 billion in annualized payment volume.

Managing group expenses frequently leaves a single organizer responsible for calculating shares, tracking incoming transfers, and chasing late payers. According to Ziina’s internal user research, asking friends to settle up represents the biggest friction point in shared spending—with some respondents noting they would rather absorb an expense than repeatedly remind peers to pay. Furthermore, 71 per cent of surveyed consumers reported splitting expenses at least once a month, while all interviewed participants indicated they rely on WhatsApp to coordinate shared bills across disconnected channels.

Automating Reminders and Cross-Platform Settlements

Split Bill centralizes expense division, payment requests, and automated follow-ups within a single interface. Available for purchases made using a Ziina Card as well as external payment methods, the feature allows organizers to allocate specific shares to each participant and monitor real-time settlement progress.

Key operational capabilities of the feature include:

In-App and Guest Checkout: Existing Ziina account holders can settle their share directly inside the mobile app, while non-users can pay via a dedicated web link using a debit card, Apple Pay, or Google Pay.

Automated Follow-Ups: The platform automatically dispatches payment reminders to outstanding participants, removing the social friction of manual follow-ups from the organizer.

Real-Time Tracking: Organizers can view individual contribution statuses as funds arrive and receive instant notifications once the entire group bill has been settled.

“We build products around real customer behaviour, identifying opportunities to make familiar financial interactions simpler and more intuitive,” stated Faisal Toukan, CEO and co-founder of Ziina. “Our user research showed us that asking friends to pay can be the hardest part of splitting an expense. With Split Bill, we’re addressing that everyday friction by making it easier for people to organise shared expenses, track contributions and settle up.”

Surging P2P Velocity and Smaller-Value Group Transfers

The launch capitalizes on rapid growth in everyday P2P activity across Ziina’s user base. During the first ten months of 2026, total P2P transfers on the platform climbed 330 per cent year-on-year, while the number of active senders and recipients grew by 220 per cent. Monthly P2P transfer volumes also recorded seven consecutive months of growth between April and October 2026.

Underlying transaction metrics point directly toward higher-frequency, everyday group spending:

Shift to Micro-Transfers: Ziina’s median P2P payment value declined by 33 per cent year-on-year, while the share of transfers valued at AED 200 or less increased by 16 per cent.

Spike in Multi-Party Settlements: Between August and October 2026, instances of users receiving payments from two or more friends on the same day surged 500 per cent year-on-year, accounting for 10 per cent of all P2P transfers executed on the platform.

UAE Digital P2P Momentum and Full-Stack Scale

Ziina’s product expansion aligns with a broader structural shift away from cash across the Emirates. Central Bank of the UAE (CBUAE) data recorded 114.9 million customer-to-customer transfers in 2025, up from 109.7 million in 2024. Meanwhile, Visa’s 2026 Where Cash Hides study revealed that digital adoption within the P2P category rose by five percentage points to reach 35 per cent.

Founded in 2020 by Faisal Toukan, Sarah Toukan, and Talal Toukan—and recently recognized with the 2026 Dubai-it Award presented by His Highness Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Crown Prince of Dubai—Ziina operates under CBUAE regulatory authorizations spanning Stored Value Facilities, Retail Payment Services Category III, and Exchange Business Category IV. By pairing licensed payment infrastructure with social, behavior-led features like Split Bill, the company continues to consolidate everyday consumer spending and merchant acquiring into a unified financial ecosystem.

FCA to explore quantum computing to tackle financial crime

              

  

  

  
    

        

    

      

A new initiative will bring together firms, quantum technology providers, and national research labs to explore practical applications of quantum computing.

  

            						

The FCA will bring together financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories to explore how quantum computing could help tackle financial crime.

The Quantum Experimentation Group, the first of its kind for a regulator, will initially explore how quantum machine learning could help detect money laundering and fraud. It will launch in the first quarter of 2027.

Participants will use an FCA synthetic dataset – artificially generated data – to help overcome a key barrier to testing: access to suitable data.

The group will help firms explore practical uses of quantum computing in financial services and share findings to guide future testing. It will also help the FCA understand the technology’s opportunities and limitations, barriers to experimentation and what these could mean for regulation.

Jessica Rusu, chief data, information and intelligence officer at the FCA, said: 'We want to help firms explore where quantum could make a meaningful difference, and early experimentation is essential to understanding its potential in financial services. By bringing together firms, technology providers and researchers we can build readiness and identify practical applications for common industry challenges, starting with financial crime.'

The initiative builds on the FCA’s research into the long-term potential of quantum computing in financial services.

Financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories can register their interest in joining the group by 31 December 2026.

Notes to editors

Read more about the Quantum Experimentation Group and how to register an interest in joining the group.

The FCA’s Quantum Experimentation Group will be the world’s first regulator-led quantum computing experimentation group.

The group will support organisations at different stages of their quantum journey, from those beginning to explore potential use cases to those already undertaking advanced experimentation.

As part of the initiative, the FCA will define problem statements and work alongside participants to build understanding of the opportunities, limitations and practical considerations associated with quantum technologies.

The initiative will complement wider activity across the UK’s quantum ecosystem by creating additional opportunities for collaborative experimentation and learning.

title: Singapore FinTech Festival Gets to Grips with AI, Digital Money and Financial Inclusion
snippet: Georgia Hanias reports from Singapore FinTech Festival, where banks are embracing blockchain and AI is raising new questions about the future of money and inclusion. The post Singapore FinTech Festival Gets to Grips with AI, Digital Money and Financial Inclusion appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Day one of Singapore FinTech Festival and there’s already a lot to talk about. AI agents making payments on our behalf, banks experimenting with blockchain-based settlement, and new ways of getting finance to small businesses that have struggled to access traditional lending.

There are some exciting ideas being discussed.. but how will any of it actually work?

Organised by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and the Global Finance and Technology Network (GFTN), the three-day festival is bringing together thousands of delegates from around the world to share their ideas about the future of financial services.

But how much of the conversation will actually be meaningful enough to cut through the usual corporate clichés around inclusion and safeguarding that usually permeate these conferences?

Fortunately, so far, quite a lot.

What’s particularly interesting is how the conversations around AI, digital money and financial inclusion are coming together. For years, we’ve heard about blockchain challenging the banks. Now we’re hearing about banks using blockchain themselves, while AI could soon be making decisions about how our money moves. And all this while millions of people and small businesses still struggle to access financial services.

Banks and blockchain are finding common ground

Yang Peng, CEO of Ant International, had plenty to say about where digital payments are heading. His company is working on a global payment network connecting digital wallets, with a particular interest in using blockchain-backed tokenised bank deposits, or what he calls ‘settlement tokens’, rather than conventional stablecoins.

But for Peng, the important thing isn’t necessarily the blockchain technology itself.

“The most important thing is not the ledger itself of blockchain, but the compliance and the asset [that] runs on this technology to prove it is a real settlement,” he explained.

By giving banks and financial institutions access to blockchain settlement, Peng believes the traditional financial sector can gain greater control over payments.

He also sees AI playing a big role, eventually working behind the scenes to find the fastest and cheapest way to move money. And he’s particularly keen for smaller businesses to benefit from better access to payments.

“This is what we all want to see,” he said.

There’s a lot to consider here, particularly as decentralised finance and traditional banking begin to find more common ground. The possibilities for faster, cheaper payments are exciting, but what happens when AI agents start making those decisions independently?

It’s something central bankers are already thinking about.

AI ambitions come with a few warnings

Professor Joachim Nagel, president of the Deutsche Bundesbank, was quite open about the uncertainty surrounding AI.

“Nobody knows what is next. AI is a disruptive technology, so every aspect of our lives is being – and will continue to be – influenced.”

He also highlighted the uncertainty caused by geopolitical conflicts, describing the difficulties facing the world economy.

“We are living in a very complicated world with so many new geopolitical conflicts. Fourteen years ago, things were much better. These are difficult times.”

Denmark’s central bank Governor Ulrik Nødgaard shares his enthusiasm for the potential of AI but warned that “circuit breakers around markets will be used more often” as autonomous systems become more powerful.

When AI agents can execute transactions at extraordinary speed, financial institutions will need to be one step ahead of what those systems are capable of doing.

Still, Nødgaard was confident about the industry’s ability to respond, reminding delegates that “our central bankers are innovators.”

And it’s not just central banks preparing for the changes ahead.

Singapore puts AI and human intelligence to work 

Singapore is taking a particularly ambitious approach to AI. In a persuasive and thoughtful opening keynote, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong highlighted the importance of combining AI with human intelligence to make financial services work for everyone. He also announced three national AI missions to help achieve that ambition.

The first tackles financial crime, encouraging banks to securely pool and share transaction data so AI can identify scams that might otherwise go unnoticed.

The second focuses on SME lending. Using AI to assess a wider range of information could help lenders identify businesses that might be overlooked because they lack a formal credit history.

The third looks ahead to agentic transactions, establishing safeguards and accountability for a future in which AI agents increasingly make payments on behalf of customers.

GFTN | Singapore FinTech Festival

If there’s one place that stands a high chance of achieving these goals, it’s definitely Singapore. With a hands-on approach to AI education for its citizens, the country is already helping people develop the skills to make better use of the technology, including in financial services.

Singapore certainly seems determined to make these plans happen, and it’s good to see regulators taking such an active role in developing the technology.

Maha El Dimachki, managing director at GFTN, also questioned the old adage that “the US innovates, Europe regulates, and Asia imitates.”

We are all innovators, she suggests, but only time will tell whether innovation will be enough to create a more inclusive financial system.

But are people actually benefiting from digital finance?

For all the exciting developments in AI and digital money, there are still some very basic problems to solve.

Hari Menon, president of global growth and opportunity at the Gates Foundation, raised a good point about the way we measure financial inclusion.

“While global account ownership has reached 75%, it is premature to declare victory in the financial inclusion race when fewer than half of adults in emerging markets actually use those accounts to make payments or grow a business,” he said.

It’s easy to celebrate the number of people with bank accounts or digital wallets, but what happens once those accounts are opened?

Menon wants the industry to move away from counting digital wallets and focus instead on how people are actually using financial services. He talked about moving people from a digital highway into a “land of usage.”

And some basic problems still need solving.

Rwanda’s High Commissioner to Singapore, Innocent B. Muhizi, pointed out that despite 94 per cent mobile coverage in Rwanda, 20 per cent of phones are still basic devices, while many people don’t know how to use mobile apps.

Airtel Mobile Commerce chairman Ari Sarker also warned against simply introducing new technology without changing the processes behind existing services.

“The biggest mistake is adopting the latest technology without changing processes,” he said.

Menon offered a much more meaningful way to measure progress.

“Progress will be made when smallholder farmers know exactly what, when and where to plant their crops” and “when women see their incomes rise,” he said.

Given that small businesses are the backbone of every global economy and women make up half the world’s population and a significant part of the agricultural workforce, measuring outcomes through their quality of life seems like a pretty good place to start.

And one of the biggest ways to make a difference is helping entrepreneurs get access to finance.

Making better use of the data we’ve got

Small businesses have always faced challenges when trying to secure funding, particularly those without a formal credit history.

Alfonso Garcia Mora, vice president at the International Finance Corporation (IFC), explained just how difficult this can be in emerging markets.

“60% of SMEs in emerging markets do not use digital payments. So they are not visible. You don’t have data as a lender to assess if the micro enterprise is good or bad,” he explained during a conversation with CNBC Asia’s Manisha Tank.

But there is lots of information out there that could help.

Garcia Mora pointed to platforms such as Grab and Mercado Libre, which are using merchant data to assess businesses and provide loans at scale.

They have “hundreds of thousands of micro-entrepreneurs” using their platforms, and much more information about those businesses than “any traditional lender will ever have.”

And this brings us back to why AI, digital finance and traditional banking need to work together.

If fintechs can use alternative data to assess businesses, banks can provide funding and regulators can develop secure open finance frameworks, there is a real opportunity to make lending accessible to entrepreneurs who have struggled to get support.

But Garcia Mora believes the industry needs to stop approaching the problem from separate perspectives. Banks, fintechs, regulators, digital platforms and international institutions all have a part to play.

And the scale of the problem is enormous.

According to the World Bank Group, micro, small and medium-sized enterprises in developing countries face a $4trillion finance gap, despite accounting for 90 per cent of businesses and 75 per cent of employment in those economies.

It’s an extraordinary figure when you consider how much technology and data we already have at our disposal.

If we use the data out there, we can truly help close the lending gap. But digital technology and mobile connectivity alone will never solve the problem unless we also find ways to support the entrepreneurs who need it most.

“There is no way we can have an impact if we don’t put all these pieces together,” said Garcia Mora.

So what are we taking away from day one? 

What I find encouraging about the conversations in Singapore so far is how many of these ideas are beginning to connect.

Banks are exploring blockchain-based settlement, AI could soon decide how payments move around the world, and new approaches to data could help businesses access finance that has traditionally been out of reach.

There’s certainly plenty of innovation to get excited about.

But the discussions about financial inclusion are an important reminder of what we’re trying to achieve. Millions of people have digital wallets they barely use, while businesses that could be creating jobs and supporting local economies still struggle to get funding.

We have the technology to move money around the world in seconds and are developing AI systems that can make financial decisions on our behalf. Surely we can also find better ways to help a small business get a loan?

Garcia Mora summed it up nicely when he said every entrepreneur should have the chance to try to realise their dream.

And if the technology being discussed in Singapore can help make that happen, it will be something worth celebrating. And that’s only day one. Two more to go.

title: After Money20/20 Middle East, The Question Is What Follows Access
snippet: Vennre's Ziad Mabsout argues that giving people more ways to invest was only the first step, and that wealth platforms must now show them the whole portfolio. The post After Money20/20 Middle East, The Question Is What Follows Access appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
The region’s investors have moved from saving into investing, helped by a growing choice of platforms and products. Writing after Money20/20 Middle East, one wealth platform founder argues that the market is still underestimating what those investors will need next.

Ziad Mabsout, Co-Founder & CEO, Vennre

Ziad Mabsout is Co-Founder and CEO of Vennre. In this contributed piece, written after Money20/20 Middle East, he sets out his own view of what the region’s wealth platforms will need to offer once access to investing is no longer the hard part. The views are his own.

This year’s Money20/20 Middle East was a good measure of how far the regional fintech ecosystem continues to develop. The progress companies have made over the past year stood out, as did the number of founders, investors and operators who are still actively building in the market.

One of the main discussions was the shift from saving to investing, and what the next generation of investors will expect from wealth platforms. AI and tokenisation will clearly play a part in that. But in Mabsout’s view, the market is still underestimating something more basic: what has to come after access.

Access changes the questions

Giving people more ways to invest is useful. Once they actually start investing, however, the questions they face are different ones. Are they allocating the right amount? Are they properly diversified? How does one investment fit alongside everything else they already own? And what should the next decision be?

Those questions do not go away because a product is easy to buy. If anything, they become harder to answer as people hold more investments in more places. That, Mabsout argues, is where the regional wealth market is heading.

The next six to 12 months

Over the next six to 12 months, he expects investors to pay much more attention to how their portfolios are actually constructed across different asset classes and platforms.

Many people have already made the move from saving into investing. The next stage is being able to step back and judge whether those individual decisions, taken one at a time, are collectively moving them towards their financial objectives. A set of sensible choices made in isolation does not automatically add up to a sensible portfolio.

What wealth platforms will need to provide

That shift changes what wealth platforms have to offer. Personalisation matters, and so does access to differentiated investment opportunities and to liquidity. But investors also need a clearer view of the portfolio as a whole, rather than of each holding on its own.

Private markets make this particularly important. Technology can make the investment journey easier and more personalised, but it does not remove the need to source and assess opportunities properly, or to decide whether they are suitable for the investor in question. As Mabsout puts it: “You still need both a strong investment engine and a strong technology engine.”

In other words, a slick interface is no substitute for the work of choosing what goes on the shelf, and that work is of limited use if investors cannot see how a new holding fits with what they already have.

Trust is part of the offer

There is a trust element to this as well. As investing becomes more digital and more accessible, the role of a wealth platform cannot simply be to make more products available. Adding choice without helping people use it well risks leaving them with more decisions and less clarity.

The next phase, Mabsout argues, will be about helping investors make sense of the choices in front of them: understanding what they already own, where they may have too much or too little exposure, and what an additional investment would actually contribute to the portfolio.

Platforms that can answer those questions will be doing something different from those that only widen the menu. For an investor, the difference is between being able to buy more and being able to see whether buying more is the right next step.

As he concludes: “Access has been an important first step for the region. The more interesting question now is what investors do with it.”

fullText:
New resource brings together real-world examples of AI adoption across financial services, helping firms identify emerging trends and opportunities.

  

            						

The FCA has launched a world-first AI Spotlight Observatory that provides firms, academics and innovators with a comprehensive view of how AI is being adopted across financial services.

Based on practical use cases from more than 200 organisations and spanning 150 areas of activity, the online platform highlights how firms are using AI across the industry and where trends are developing.

Developed in partnership with the Centre for Finance, Technology and Entrepreneurship (CFTE) and technology partner NayaOne, the Observatory helps meet the growing demand for greater visibility of AI adoption across the sector.

The resource highlights a range of AI use cases shaping financial services, from solutions designed to combat financial crime and enhance compliance processes to emerging technologies such as agentic payments and neurosymbolic AI.

By widening access to market intelligence, the Observatory will help firms of all sizes learn from developments across the market, better understand emerging technologies and make more informed decisions about adopting AI responsibly. 

Jessica Rusu, chief data, information and intelligence officer at the FCA, said: 'AI is creating significant opportunities across financial services, and we’re committed to helping firms understand how the technology is being used.

'The AI Spotlight Observatory provides an open and accessible resource that brings together real-world examples of AI adoption, helping firms, innovators and researchers learn from developments across the sector and identify new opportunities for innovation and growth.'

Notes to editors

The FCA’s AI Spotlight Observatory is the first resource of its kind for a regulator globally.  

It builds on the FCA’s AI Spotlight Digital Showcase, a repository of practical AI solutions across specific themes, by adding new features and capabilities, such as a common taxonomy for comparison, a distinction between use cases and implementations, and the ability to identify emerging patterns across the market. 

The platform is open and accessible to all users. Registration is required to access more detailed insights, such as target client information, and to request demonstrations directly from innovators featured on the platform. 

The Observatory will continue to evolve through the addition of new use cases. Firms can apply to be showcased on the platform.

CFTE has supported the development of the Observatory across three main areas: creating the taxonomy, building the repository, and socialising the Observatory with the market.  

The Observatory forms part of CFTE’s wider collaboration with the FCA on AI capability, industry engagement and market intelligence. Alongside initiatives such as the Agentic Academy, CFTE supports the FCA in helping the financial-services sector better understand, structure and respond to the opportunities and challenges created by AI. 

NayaOne has been responsible for the design and development of the Observatory platform, including the user interface, navigation, search and filtering capabilities. 

The platform builds on the FCA’s wider work on AI, including its  

AI Discussion Paper, AI Sprint, and AI Lab, which includes AI Live Testing and its groundbreaking Supercharged Sandbox supported by NVIDIA, NayaOne and Anthropic. 

Last month, the FCA published examples of AI good practice and areas of improvement to support the safe and responsible adoption of AI in financial services.

title: From wallet to full-stack fintech: Murtaza Ali on JazzCash’s path to 2030
snippet: Murtaza Ali, CEO of JazzCash, on 64 million users, lending, insurance and government payments in Pakistan, and the road to 2030. The Fintech Times SFF 2026 cover story. The post From wallet to full-stack fintech: Murtaza Ali on JazzCash’s path to 2030 appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Mobile money has shown it can reach people with no bank account. The harder test in emerging markets is whether it can then give them credit, insurance and savings, and carry government payments too. 

In Pakistan, JazzCash has become one of the clearest answers, growing from a basic mobile wallet into a platform that handles payments, lending, insurance, merchant services and government disbursements at national scale.

Operating as a standalone entity and partnering with Mobilink Microfinance Bank, JazzCash is a core pillar of VEON’s digital operator strategy. It was recently named among the World’s Top Fintech Companies 2026 by CNBC and Statista in the Payments category.

In this exclusive interview, Murtaza Ali, CEO of JazzCash, discusses the platform’s evolution, the shift to a cashless economy, the role of lending, insurance and social protection in financial inclusion, and the road to becoming a full-stack fintech by 2030.

This interview is the cover story of The Fintech Times Singapore Fintech Festival 2026 Special Edition, distributed at Singapore EXPO from 18 to 20 November 2026. Read the full edition here. 

JazzCash began in 2012 as a basic mobile wallet. How would you describe the journey to where the platform stands today?

It has been a steady expansion of what customers needed from us. In the early years the focus was on fundamentals: money transfers, and bill payments. Once that foundation was trusted, we moved into merchant acquiring, digital payments, consumer lending, remittances and a debit card. From there we added a payment gateway, insurance, merchant lending, buy now pay later and cross-border payments.

Today JazzCash serves 64 million users, and one in three adults in Pakistan uses it. None of this was built in isolation. We built each product around a task people already did in cash or in queues, and made it work from a phone.

We did not set out to build a long list of products. We set out to solve the next real problem for the customer.

JazzCash processes the equivalent of 16% of Pakistan’s GDP and one in every three e-commerce payments. What explains this level of adoption?

Trust and convenience, built on a distribution network that is hard to replicate. Our agent and merchant footprint puts JazzCash within reach of people who have never had a bank branch nearby. On top of that, we process more than 16 million transactions a day, up 68% year on year, so reliability has to be constant.

E-commerce is a good example. JazzCash has 2,000+ online merchants including food delivery, ticketing and marketplaces. As volumes grow, so does our responsibility to know who is using the platform. Every merchant and aggregator goes through KYC and due diligence under State Bank of Pakistan rules, and transactions are monitored continuously. Customers don’t choose a payment method for the technology behind it. They choose the one that works every time.

More volume means more responsibility. Every merchant is verified and monitored.

Pakistan is pushing towards a cashless economy. What role does the merchant network play?

It is fundamental, because a wallet is only useful if there are places to spend from it. Pakistan has fewer than 200,000 card terminals for over 250 million people, and a card terminal rarely makes sense for a small roadside (kiryana) store or a home-based business. A printed or digital QR code does, with no hardware at all.

We now have 1.9 million merchants and over 8 million active QR users. We hold a significant volume of RAAST person-to-merchant QR payments, and monthly throughput has grown seven times. More than half of our merchants are onboarded through digital channels, and for those who need guidance, field teams help them get started under the same compliance standards. This work sits within the Prime Minister’s Cashless Economy Initiative, and our Chairman, Aamir Ibrahim, serves on the Prime Minister’s Task Force on Cashless Economy.

When a shopkeeper goes digital, the whole neighbourhood economy moves with them.

Digital lending is often seen as risky in emerging markets. How is JazzCash approaching it?

Carefully, and at scale. We issue more than 280,000 loans every day on an average, and our ReadyCash product won Silver for Banking at Money20/20 USA 2025. Over four million customers use the lending product each month, and 30% of borrowers are women.

These are small, short-term loans that help a household cover an emergency or a small business buy stock. Payments and wallet data help us lend to people the traditional system could not assess. The aim is to build credit history for people who had none, so responsible borrowing leads to better access over time.

Credit works best when it is small, fast, and built on a customer’s own financial behaviour.

Insurance penetration in Pakistan is below 1% of GDP, yet JazzCash sold over 1.3 million policies in a single day. What does that tell us?

That the demand for protection was always there. What was missing was a product that was simple, affordable and available where people already transact. Health insurance in Pakistan has traditionally been tied to formal employment, yet around 75% of the workforce is informal, and most private health spending, about 89%, is paid out of pocket. For a household with no savings buffer, one bad diagnosis can undo years of progress.

So we embedded insurance into the app and into everyday transactions, with products starting from PKR 3 a day, around one US cent, and the Sehat+ health platform backed by nearly 400 panel hospitals. During the 2025 monsoon floods, more than 43,000 policyholders received an instant relief payment directly in their wallets, the first digital claim payout of its kind in Pakistan. Today we reach 17.9 million policyholders and are the number one digital insurance distribution platform in the country, recognised as a winner for InsurTech at The Money Awards 2026.

Financial inclusion is not complete until people are protected, not just banked.

JazzCash is also a major partner for channelling government stipends and welfare. How did that come about?

It started with disaster relief for displaced families in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in 2021, and grew through our selection as a disbursement partner for the Benazir Income Support Programme, Pakistan’s largest social safety net. BISP pays a stipend to a woman in 12 million low-income households, and for years collecting it meant travelling to a campsite, spending around 10% of the grant on the commute, proving identity in person.

We rebuilt that journey. Beneficiaries are verified with CNIC and biometric checks, receive a free Jazz SIM pre-linked to a wallet, and the money lands directly in their own account. Direct wallet transfers have already reached PKR 20 billion for 1.48 million women, with no agent, no queue and no wait. Across all our government and development sector partnerships we serve more than 3 million beneficiaries, channelling over PKR 100 billion this year alone.

Getting paid should not cost a day’s wages. Dignity is part of the design.

Financial inclusion and poverty alleviation are central to the VEON narrative. What impact are you seeing?

For many customers, JazzCash is the first formal financial service they use, and women hold 35% of our accounts. For many beneficiaries, a government stipend is their first step into the digital economy, and the wallet then becomes a place to save, pay, borrow and get insured.

Poverty alleviation is not one product. It is access to a safe place to save, a way to receive money, credit to start or grow something, and insurance to protect it. When those come through one platform on a phone a person already owns, the barriers fall quickly.

Access to financial services is a foundation for a better life.

What lessons from JazzCash apply to VEON’s other markets?

The core lesson is to start with the customer’s daily need and build around the distribution you already have. Across VEON, 59 million active customers now use our financial services in Pakistan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, and Bangladesh is set to join with regulatory progress there.

Each market is at a different stage, but the playbook travels well: payments first, then the ecosystem around it. The value comes from sharing what works across the Group, including our partnership with Mastercard to scale AI-enabled financial services across four markets.

The model is portable. The customer insight has to be local.

Looking ahead to 2030, what is the vision for JazzCash?

The JazzCash app will work like a personal financial adviser: you talk to it, and it helps you pay bills, make idle money work and borrow when you need to.

Ask “What is due today?” and you’ll see your bills in one place and pay them with one tap or a voice command. If PKR 50,000 has sat untouched since the start of the month, the app will ask whether you’d like to move it into savings or a mutual fund. If a bill falls due before your next income arrives and your balance won’t cover it, the app will offer a small loan, with the cost shown upfront.

This is hyper-personalisation: customers who have never had access to investment or credit products will have it on their own screen, at the moment it matters. For people using AI in a financial app for the first time, trust comes first, so security has to be strict and data has to stay sovereign. We will not scale these features faster than we can secure them.

Your money should not sit idle, and your app should be the first to notice.

About JazzCash

JazzCash began in 2012 as a mobile wallet and now serves 64 million users in Pakistan, with payments, lending, insurance, merchant services and government disbursements. It is part of VEON and partners with Mobilink Microfinance Bank. jazzcash.com.pk

Three themes stand out: the growing use of AI, innovation crossing traditional sector boundaries, and financial inclusion.

As firms develop new products, services and business models, many engage with us through our Regulatory Sandbox and Innovation Pathways to understand how regulation applies to their proposition or to test innovative ideas in a controlled environment.

Looking across applications lets us observe emerging trends. It helps us understand how technologies are evolving, and identify emerging regulatory questions.

In turn, this supports our wider work and helps us keep pace with developments across financial services.

Applications at a glance

37% involved AI (up from 31% in 2025), making it the most common technology theme.

92% of the firms engaging with our services were doing so for the first time, highlighting continued demand from new innovators.

64% of proposed solutions included a retail element, showing continued focus on consumer-facing innovation.

The growing use of AI

Firms are focusing increasingly on how to deploy, oversee and govern AI in their business models.

They’re looking at how to use AI to help consumers better understand and manage their finances, support businesses with payment processes, and provide customers with more personalised guidance and support.

Regulation and innovation are working in tandem to deploy new technologies safely and build consumer protection into new products from the outset.

Innovation is becoming more interconnected

Innovation does not always fit neatly into traditional sector categories. While payments and digital assets represented the largest sector-specific portion of recent applications, cross-sector propositions have also been common, representing around one-third of applications.

Many firms are combining technologies, data, payments and consumer-facing services in new ways. As a result, innovative technologies are increasingly crossing traditional sector boundaries and requiring firms to consider how existing governance, accountability, data use and regulatory frameworks apply.

A recent example is our stablecoins cohort in the Regulatory Sandbox. Stablecoin business models often cut across traditional sector boundaries, combining elements of payments, digital assets, and financial market activity. The cohort brought together firms intending to issue UK stablecoins to test how proposed requirements could operate in practice and provide evidence to support policy development.

Financial inclusion

Firms continue to focus on how to improve consumer access to and engagement with financial services. They’re not only exploring new technologies, but also considering how these tools can help address practical consumer challenges.

Applications this year have included propositions aimed at improving consumer understanding, accessibility, personalised support, and access to financial services for underserved groups.

A large proportion of proposed solutions included a retail element, indicating that most firms remain focused on end consumers.

What we’re learning about Sandbox participation over time

We are looking beyond current application trends to understand the longer-term experience of firms that have participated in the Regulatory Sandbox.

Our preliminary research suggests that, as of September 2026, around 71% of them are still active. We are continuing this analysis to better understand the ongoing commercial success of participating firms and whether their original propositions have continued to operate.

We have also been looking to understand at which point of their growth firms engage with the Regulatory Sandbox.

We’ve found that the service is particularly relevant at an early stage of a firm’s development, with around 70% of applications coming from firms that are 0 to 2 years old.

Demand is strongest when firms are still developing their business models, products and approaches to compliance, and seeking to understand how regulation applies as they refine and validate innovative propositions.

Looking ahead

Applications to our Regulatory Sandbox and Innovation Pathways give us an early view of the technologies, business models and the regulatory questions that firms are exploring.

They also provide insight into developments beyond the UK.

We’re continuing to engage with international firms seeking to enter the UK market and sharing insights with overseas regulators and innovation initiatives. This helps us to understand global innovation trends.

The trends we have seen so far suggest that innovation is scaling up, becoming more sophisticated, and more focused on addressing real-world consumer needs.

We’ll continue to engage with firms as technology develops. One way we’re doing this is through thematic cohorts, which explore key areas in greater depth.

Following our Regulatory Sandbox stablecoins cohort, applications to a new climate scenarios cohort opened on 1 October 2026. The cohort invites firms and specialists to test innovative approaches to climate scenario analysis and risk assessment, supporting wider work on sustainable finance and climate-related risks.

Firms developing new ideas should consider how existing regulation applies to their proposition, how they can test and scale innovation successfully, and what safeguards will deliver good outcomes for consumers and markets.

Our innovation services help firms answer these questions. They also let us test policy approaches and gather evidence on how regulation works in practice. This helps inform smarter, more proportionate regulation.

We’re here to support innovators across financial services, helping ensure the UK remains one of the best places in the world to develop, test and scale innovative propositions.

To find out more about our innovation services and keep up to date with future opportunities, visit our Regulatory Sandbox and Innovation Pathways pages.

title: What Indian lenders Will Ask Their Fintech Partners Under DPDP
snippet: Singahi's Rahul Verma argues that India's DPDP Act leaves lenders answerable for their partners, and sets out the questions fintechs should expect to face. The post What Indian lenders Will Ask Their Fintech Partners Under DPDP appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
India’s new data protection regime leaves banks, NBFCs and payment firms responsible for what their technology partners do with customer data. A cybersecurity specialist argues that lenders will respond by putting much tougher questions to those partners well before the main duties start in May 2027.

Rahul Verma is a Cybersecurity Sales Specialist at Singahi, which helps growing companies prove security to customers, investors and regulators. In this contributed piece he sets out his own view of what lenders and payment firms will ask their fintech partners under India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act. The views are his own.

Most of India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 applies from 13 May 2027. For banks, NBFCs and payment companies, the visible work is plain enough: consent notices, customer rights and breach reporting. Less visible, but just as demanding, is the job of checking every partner that handles customer data on their behalf.

That list runs long. A single lender might rely on one firm for video KYC, another for collection calls and a third for credit decisioning, alongside a cloud host, an SMS gateway and an outsourced support desk. Under the Act, each of those partners is a Data Processor. The lender is the Data Fiduciary, and section 8(1) keeps it responsible for what its processors do, “irrespective of any agreement to the contrary”.

“An indemnity clause doesn’t move that duty,” says Verma. Lenders cannot contract their way out of the liability, so they will do the next best thing and ask far harder questions before they sign or renew. He expects those questions to fall into six areas, each traceable to the Act or the DPDP Rules, 2025.

A contract that says the right things

Section 8(2) allows a Data Fiduciary to use a processor only under a valid contract, and Rule 6(1)(f) requires that contract to provide for reasonable security safeguards. Fintechs should expect a DPDP schedule at renewal, often placed beside the terms already written for RBI’s outsourcing rules. A partner that has never had to describe its security in contract language will now have to.

Breach notice measured in hours

Under Rule 7, the lender must tell the Board and every affected customer without delay once it becomes aware of a breach, with a fuller report to the Board within 72 hours. Banks also owe CERT-In a report within six hours for some incidents, and RBI has its own six-hour rule. A partner that sits on an incident for two days causes the lender to miss every one of those deadlines.

Verma expects the schedule to ask for a notice period in hours, and the lender’s security team to check the partner’s incident procedure against it. Where the contract says 24 hours and the procedure says 72, someone will ask which one is true.

A year of logs

Rule 6(1)(e) and Rule 8(3) call for personal data and processing logs to be retained for a year, and that covers work done by a Data Processor too. The Rules even give the example of a company whose customer records sit with a cloud provider. Partners should be ready for the lender to ask what their retention settings actually are.

Acting on withdrawn consent

This is the question most easily missed. Under section 6(6), once a customer withdraws consent the lender has a reasonable time to stop processing, and it must make its processors stop as well, except where a law requires or allows the processing to continue.

Take a marketing partner holding a few lakh customer records for a lender. One customer withdraws consent. Can the partner stop using that single record, and tell the lender the date it stopped? Section 8(7) works the same way for erasure once the purpose has been served, and at the end of a contract lenders will want the deletion confirmed in writing.

Naming the sub-processors

Lenders will want to know which sub-processors touch the data and where each one operates. A fintech running on three cloud services and an outsourced support team should be able to name them without a week of digging.

Supporting the lender’s audit

A lender notified as a Significant Data Fiduciary needs an independent data auditor, along with a yearly impact assessment and audit, under section 10(2) and Rule 13(1). Auditors follow the data, so they will want evidence from the partners that hold it, and the contract will give the lender the right to collect it.

Why the pressure will be real

The fines land on the lender. Failing to take reasonable security safeguards, including over what its processors do, can cost up to ₹250 crore. Failing to report a breach can cost up to ₹200 crore. Exposure on that scale travels down the supply chain through contract terms and questionnaires.

None of it requires a certificate. Nothing in the Act or the Rules makes ISO/IEC 27701, or any other standard, compulsory for processors. In Verma’s view, most of the answers already exist somewhere in a fintech’s contracts, cloud consoles and incident runbooks. The task is to gather them before a lender’s questionnaire arrives in, say, April 2027, a few weeks before the main duties begin.

title: Senators Urge Treasury to Protect State Stablecoin Charters Under GENIUS Act
snippet: Six senators are calling on the Treasury Department to give state stablecoin issuers equal footing with federal charters under section 3 of the GENIUS Act, they said in a Wednesday (Nov. 18) press release. Sens. Cynthia Lummis of Wyoming, Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Kevin Cramer of North Dakota, Pete Ricketts […] The post Senators Urge Treasury to Protect State Stablecoin Charters Under GENIUS Act appeared first on PYMNTS.com.
fullText:
Sens. Cynthia Lummis of Wyoming, Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Kevin Cramer of North Dakota, Pete Ricketts of Nebraska and Mark Warner of Virginia made the call in a Tuesday (Nov. 17) letter addressed to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, saying they wrote in response to Treasury’s Aug. 18 notice of proposed rulemaking on payment stablecoin issuance, offer and sale.

“For Treasury to finalize this proposal in a way that reflects Congressional intent, it must allow issuers to choose from state or federal charters, as contemplated by the GENIUS Act, without the risk of business disruption or uncertainty,” the senators wrote in the letter.

When announcing its notice of proposed rulemaking in August, the Treasury Department said it aims to provide clarity to the industry regarding when an issuer needs to obtain a GENIUS license as well as when and how payment stablecoins can be offered and sold in U.S. markets, PYMNTS reported at the time.

The senators said in their Tuesday letter that Treasury’s current proposal does not offer state stablecoin issuers the same protection it gives issuers that have pending applications to federal regulators, that this regulatory inequality may incentivize issuers to seek a federal license rather than a state one, and that Congress’s intent with the GENIUS Act was to ensure that state stablecoin regulatory regimes have parity with federal ones.

“Treasury should implement the GENIUS Act accordingly,” the senators wrote in the letter. “Establishing a robust safe harbor will preserve the dual banking system, provide regulatory certainty, promote innovation and competition, and ensure that state supervision remains an equal component of the nation’s stablecoin regulatory framework.”

Wyoming, New York and Nebraska have digital asset regulatory regimes, according to the press release.

The GENIUS Act allows stablecoin issuers with $10 billion or less in outstanding stablecoins to operate under a state regulatory regime if that regime is “substantially similar” to the federal framework. Issuers in some states that have existing digital asset regulatory regimes are not required to submit to federal supervision when they reach $10 billion, per the release.

The Conference of State Bank Supervisors said in a Wednesday post on social platform X: “CSBS appreciates the bipartisan leadership of [Lummis and Gillibrand] and colleagues urging Treasury to give state-supervised stablecoin issuers equal footing with federal issuers under the GENIUS Act. State-federal parity preserves charter choice and competition.”

CSBS appreciates the bipartisan leadership of @SenLummis, @SenGillibrand and colleagues urging Treasury to give state-supervised stablecoin issuers equal footing with federal issuers under the GENIUS Act. State-federal parity preserves charter choice and competition.

— CSBS (@CSBSNews) November 18, 2026

Kevin Wysocki, head of policy at Anchorage Digital, said in a reply to a post on X by Lummis: “I don’t think there is much [of] a safe harbor to extend state issuers. Issuers are picking the federal path. The $10B cap for state issuers—though there can be an exemption—is a risk few issuers are willing to take. There are other reasons too, but that’s the reason most related to the GENIUS Act itself.”

title: Insights2040 day two: regulators mark their own quantum homework
snippet: global toolkit showing most financial regulators are at an early stage on quantum, a payments industry report saying nobody yet owns the problem, and four questions GFTN is carrying into the Singapore Fintech Festival. The post Insights2040 day two: regulators mark their own quantum homework appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
The closed-door meetings ended with a global toolkit showing most financial regulators are at an early stage on quantum, a payments industry report saying nobody yet owns the problem, and four questions GFTN is carrying into the Singapore Fintech Festival.

The second and final day of GFTN’s Insights2040 Annual Meetings was framed by the organiser around trust, scale and operational resilience: institutions putting enterprise AI, tokenised assets and cross-border stablecoins to work while defending against AI-enabled fraud and quantum threats. Only one of the day’s sessions produced a published document, and it turned the lens on the regulators themselves.

Twenty-five regulators, graded by their own hand

The Global Financial Innovation Network published its Project Otto Toolkit after a launch session at the Sands Expo and Convention Centre. Led by the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority with the Alberta Securities Commission, the British Columbia Securities Commission and India’s IFSCA, it asked 25 member regulators to assess their own maturity on quantum, in two areas: quantum security, meaning the threat to today’s encryption, and quantum innovation, meaning what the technology could do for finance.

The method is simple to describe. Regulators were scored against 42 measures grouped by what they say, what they do and how they engage with firms, on four levels from ad hoc to adaptive. The results are anonymised and the report is careful about its limits: self-assessed, not statistically representative and not a ranking.

The picture is of an early-stage field. Most respondents sit in the lower and middle of the range. Most score higher on security than on innovation. The most mature activity is the easiest one: 84 per cent, or 21 of the 25, are beyond the lowest level on attending events. On security, 76 per cent are beyond the lowest level on horizon scanning and on building internal capability, but no security measure has a most common score in the top two levels. On innovation, the most common score for most measures is the lowest, and hands-on engagement with firms through sandboxes, testing and proofs of concept is the weakest area of all.

“Regulators are building maturity through action rather than articulation,” the report says. Of the innovation side, it is blunter: “Quantum innovation is exploratory, not experimental.”

Four examples of practice are named, among them the Dubai Financial Services Authority’s Emerging Technology Risk Regulatory College, alongside a Canadian securities regulators’ working group, IFSCA’s innovation sandbox and the FCA’s repeatable supervisory assessment of firms’ readiness for post-quantum cryptography. In his foreword, Colin Payne, head of innovation at the FCA and GFIN chair, writes: “Our challenge is not to predict the quantum future with certainty, but to ensure we are prepared to shape it responsibly.”

The industry mirror

The payments industry published its own version of the same finding on the same day. The Emerging Payments Association Asia released From Awareness to Action: What Quantum-Safe Readiness Requires Now, the work of its quantum-safe cryptography working group.

Its argument is that awareness of the risk has not turned into action because nobody inside most organisations owns it. In the association’s own workshops last year, only 20 per cent of participants said their senior stakeholders were very familiar with the threat. The report also points to the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s first Quantum Preparedness Index, which it says scored the territory’s banking sector 2.3 out of 10 in July.

The remedy is a 90-day list: name an accountable executive, start discovery in a handful of high-value systems, ask critical vendors for their post-quantum plans and dates, assess readiness across the organisation, and write cryptographic agility into contracts as they come up for renewal. “Awareness is growing, but ownership is still unclear,” said Camilla Bullock, the association’s chief executive. Payments make the problem harder than most, because every party in a chain has to move. As IBM’s Ray Harishankar put it, organisations are “only as ready as the vendors and counterparties with which they exchange messages”.

Put the two documents side by side and the week’s pattern holds. The standards exist and the cryptography exists. What is missing is someone accountable for using them.

Four bottlenecks

In its message to delegates, GFTN summarised two days of roundtables as work on four bottlenecks: how digital assets and stablecoins hold up under stress, who is accountable when autonomous AI agents transact, how to build services on top of interoperable payment rails, and how to close gaps in fraud defence and quantum readiness. It said the discussions would be carried forward across its forums in 2027.

The published agenda shows how those questions were framed. Sessions on the final day asked how cross-border stablecoin recognition can work, how tokenisation moves beyond issuance, who is accountable in an economy of AI agents and whether convertibility can hold under stress at scale. None of them is a question about whether the technology functions.

The Singapore Fintech Festival opens on Wednesday at Singapore EXPO, with Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong giving the ministerial keynote. The questions from the closed rooms now move to the public stages.

title: Superintelligence may still be years away. AI agents inside bank accounts aren’t.
snippet: AI agents are emerging as a cybersecurity risk for financial institutions, with their ability to exploit vulnerabilities and access bank accounts highlighting the need for stronger controls over autonomous payments. The post Superintelligence may still be years away. AI agents inside bank accounts aren’t. appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
The day after the Binance hack that took place October 29th, Elon Musk did what Elon Musk does best. He posted about it.

On X, he said: “Super intelligence agents will at some point do this to gain currency for themselves, not a human,”

He was referring to a clever move made by the hacker during the attack. Before issuers had the chance to freeze any stablecoins, hackers moved around $60m in stolen USDT into a crypto lending platform. Then, used it as collateral to borrow around $44.6m worth of Ether.

Reason being, issuers can freeze USDT (and that’s exactly what Tether and Circle did to a large chunk). They cannot, however, do the same to Ether in the same way. So by swapping one for the other, the attacker found a way to move money beyond reach.

Musk’s point was that if a human can spot and exploit a weakness like this, an intelligent enough AI agent will eventually be able to do so too, and it won’t necessarily be working for a human but instead acting in its own interests.

The more I looked into it, the more I realised we might be a lot closer to Musk’s prediction becoming reality than I’d like to think. Here’s why…

Washington already says it’s here

Back in September, the White House signed an executive order telling federal agencies to stop using the term ‘artificial intelligence’ and, instead, start calling it Super Intelligence.

The order defines Super Intelligence using the same legal definition as artificial intelligence. So this is essentially just semantics, not a declaration that superintelligence has arrived. It does, however, mean that the US government has begun using Musk’s terminology in its own guides and documents.

So what about the technology itself? Are we actually close?

Last month, Deutsche Bank‘s Research Institute looked at a theory known as the San Francisco Consensus. It’s the belief, one shared by many over at Silicon Valley, that AI will eventually start accelerating its own development and potentially reaching superintelligence by 2030.

Researchers haven’t ruled this possibility out, though they have pointed to some obstacles, including scientific uncertainty and the enormous amount of electricity and computing power that would be required.

But I think we’re getting distracted by the end goal here. Because you don’t need a machine that’s smarter than every human to create serious problems for banks and other financial institutions. All you need is an AI agent that can spot a weakness, then act on it by moving money before anyone notices. That technology exists today.

The bots are already in the accounts

Almost a year ago, Anthropic published research showing that AI agents could find and exploit weaknesses in real cryptocurrency smart contracts in a simulation.

In just 12 months, the share of recent attacks they could successfully carry out rose from 2% to more than half. Finding weaknesses in a contract cost as little as $1.22.

I want to be clear here about what this means. This isn’t a prediction made by a tech billionaire on what AI might be capable of in the future. This research was proof of what these systems can actually do, right now, in a controlled environment.

Then, on 22 October, Axios reported that some of America’s biggest banks were discovering unapproved AI agents inside customer accounts. I’ve recently gotten really into using AI-bots myself, using them, both for streamlining my work, and automating my personal life. There was a time whereby the bot platform I use asked if I wanted it to access my banking information. I, of course, did not allow it access. That doesn’t seem to be the case for everyone using these bots.

Axios found, customers had willingly given AI bots access to their own banking information. Bots had logged in using customers’ own passwords. Some even appeared to be carrying out transactions or other actions that customers hadn’t actually requested.

Banks moved quickly to restrict access. Morgan Stanley began blocking third-party AI agents, although it said it hadn’t found any rogue agents itself. JPMorgan, Bank of America and Citi also tightened restrictions on access to their systems.

Freezes work, just not fast enough

Back to the Binance hack. The industry’s response, to its credit, was really strong. I wrote about this recently because I was really impressed by how quickly stablecoin issuers stepped in to freeze the stolen funds. Without those freezes, the losses could have been considerably worse.

However, while the first freeze came in under an hour, it was still after attackers made the Aave trade and a large chunk of the money had moved beyond reach. The FBI has since blamed North Korean hackers for the attack. People, in other words, using automated tools to move quickly and exploit opportunities as they appeared.

That’s what worries me because, if a human-operated team using AI can get that far in 40 minutes, how much could an AI agent achieve in the same amount of time?

Regulators are asking the right question

The most useful thing I’ve read on this came from America’s national bank regulator, the OCC. On November 4th, it published a framework telling its examiners how to judge banks’ use of super intelligence.

Its big idea is that the risk shouldn’t be based on how clever an AI is, but what it’s allowed to do. A chatbot that drafts internal memos sits in the lowest risk tier, for instance. A fully autonomous agent that can send payments, in contrast, sits in the highest however well it does in testing.

The OCC makes a point I think everyone in payments should take seriously. An agent doesn’t have to be hacked to cause damage. It can be running perfectly and still do something it should never have been allowed to do.

In a survey of 230 US banking professionals this spring, 72% said their institution is not prepared to shut down an AI system that goes wrong, or to report the failure to regulators.

Here’s what I’d do to prepare for these occasions:

Know every agent on your rails: That includes your own, as well as your vendors’ and customers’. Know what each one can touch.

Give agents an identity and limit: Every agent that can move money should be tied to a verified owner, with spending limits you can change or revoke.

Build brakes that don’t wait for a human: Limits that stop unusual payments automatically, with a person signing off anything big that can’t be reversed.

Test your kill switch: On a system that looks like it’s working fine.

Agree the response in advance: Banks, exchanges and issuers. All should know who calls who before something happens, not during.

At some point

Musk said superintelligent agents would do this “at some point” and I personally think he may be right. But, I also don’t think that this matters as much as what’s already happening today.

Because AI bots are already logging into banks. They’re already using tools to find their weaknesses, tools that can cost as little as a dollar.

Our best response to a $6.3bn theft still started with someone noticing and reporting it quickly.

The real test of financial security won’t be how much we freeze after the fact. It’ll be how little we let leave in the first place.

title: SFF day one: the technology works, the hard part is everyone else
snippet: The Singapore Fintech Festival opened with three national AI missions, a formal launch for the Future of Finance Institute and a roadmap for PayNow. The post SFF day one: the technology works, the hard part is everyone else appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
The Singapore Fintech Festival opened with three national AI missions, a formal launch for the Future of Finance Institute and a roadmap for PayNow. On the Policy Stage, central bankers from five jurisdictions agreed that connecting the world’s payment systems is now a question of governance, not engineering.

The eleventh Singapore Fintech Festival opened at Singapore EXPO on Wednesday with the organisers promising that the decade of pilots is ending. By the close of the first day that looked less like a slogan than a summary. Almost every announcement, and almost every panel, was about who is responsible once the technology is switched on.

Three missions and a shared view of scams

Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong, who chairs the Monetary Authority of Singapore, used the ministerial keynote to announce three National AI Missions for Financial Services: strengthening financial crime prevention, improving access to financing for businesses, and enabling AI agents to transact safely.

The first is the furthest along. Five banks are already pooling transaction data in a proof-of-value, so that AI models can find patterns no single bank can see, and MAS will begin a design study early next year for an industry-wide Scam Detection Utility, including how it would be governed and run. “Scams are not confined within the boundary of one bank,” he said. “We will not be able to mitigate the risk if each institution sees only its part of the transaction chain.”

The case for pooling had been made that morning by the private sector. LexisNexis Risk Solutions reported that four Singapore banks sharing device-level intelligence through its network helped identify 461,562 fraudulent payments worth S$2.6 billion in 2025, almost half of them moved through money mule accounts.

On AI agents, the Deputy Prime Minister set the terms plainly. “Agents must operate within defined authority and limits,” he said, and “financial institutions must remain accountable, with strong human oversight and effective safeguards.”

The machinery for the missions was unveiled alongside them. The Future of Finance Institute, the public-private body MAS set up earlier this year, was formally launched with DBS, OCBC, Standard Chartered and UOB as launch partners. It will run an AI Innovation Arena, which gives developers synthetic data built from the five banks’ pooled transactions, and an Agentic Money Sandbox, where financial institutions can test AI agents making payments and managing treasury with digital money before anything goes live.

PayNow opens up

MAS and the Association of Banks in Singapore also published the implementation roadmap for PayNow Generation 2. Its centrepiece is a new SGQR+ switch that will let any licensed payment app scan any QR code, with a limited rollout in 2027 and a wider one in 2028. Higher-value payments to government agencies follow from late 2027, common rules for disputes, refunds and scams in 2028, and MAS will publish a Future Payment Rails Blueprint next year.

Anyone wondering how an incumbent feels about that kind of opening got an answer on the Policy Stage. Alan Ni, chief executive of TNG Digital, described the day Malaysia’s central bank told Touch ’n Go to open the two million small merchants it had spent heavily to sign up to every rival wallet and bank, for free. It sounded like a disaster. Five years on, he said, it may be the best thing that happened to the company: QR payments in Malaysia have grown by about 60 per cent a year and last year overtook credit and debit cards. His advice to regulators was to mind the commercials as well as the rules, because the private sector will not show up otherwise.

“Technology is not a problem”

The afternoon’s cross-border sessions made the day’s argument in so many words. On a panel of central bankers moderated by MAS’s Alan Lim, Miguel Díaz, deputy head of the BIS Innovation Hub, said the Hub had now tested three different ways of connecting payment systems across borders: tokenised ledgers, synchronisation between existing systems, and hub-and-spoke links between instant payment schemes. “Technology is not a problem,” he said. “All the three technologies work marvellously well.” What needs far more work is governance and agreeing a common set of rules.

Ivan Odonnat, general director for financial stability and operations at the Banque de France, agreed. “Technology is not the issue. The issue is governance.” Project Agora, the cross-border wholesale payments project involving around 50 commercial banks, has been through real-value testing and will go live, he said, but whether that is the end of 2027 or 2028 depends on how the governance is arranged.

Dr Alexandra Hachmeister, director general for the digital euro at Deutsche Bundesbank, offered Monday’s Project Simbolon as proof. Two central banks, two commercial banks and a technology provider settled euros against Singapore dollars atomically, and the much-discussed shared ledger was not required. “We did not need one,” she said.

There were dates, too. Tom Mutton, the Bank of England’s executive director of payments innovation and Fintech, said the Bank will set out a tokenisation roadmap at an event on 7 December, covering both assets and the cash leg, and will take its synchronisation service live in 2028. Odonnat said France’s tokenised commercial paper market goes live in December, with issuers representing about 60 per cent of the outstanding amount on board. The lesson from that project was not technical either: what built confidence was knowing settlement would be in central bank money.

An earlier panel on regional blocs heard the same thing from three continents. José Beltrán, board chair of Nexus Global Payments, called technical interoperability “probably the simplest part”; the work is in operating rules, contractual certainty, liability and supervision. Clara Arthur, chief executive of Ghana’s interbank payment system GhIPSS, said the obstacle in Africa is fragmented regulation between central banks, and pointed to the Fintech passport Ghana and Rwanda have agreed as the way through. “Payment is about trust,” she said. Carrie Suen of Ant International, whose Alipay+ network links 53 wallets, put it most directly: “It’s not just the tech, but really down to the human level, the trust, the mutual respect, and also the share of accountability.”

When the rule is in the money

If rules are to be written into money itself, someone still has to answer for them. Dr Eva Hüpkes, secretary general of the International Association of Deposit Insurers, drew the line that matters to customers. A tokenised deposit is an ordinary bank deposit recorded on a programmable ledger and is protected like one. A token that changes hands without the bank knowing who holds it is not a deposit. And either way, “deposit insurers provide protection when the bank fails, but not when the code fails.”

Odonnat supplied the cautionary tale. In a test under the BIS’s Project Mandala, which puts proof of compliance checks on chain, the sanctions list being applied turned out to be out of date, and the system raised no alert. His conclusion was that the institution applying an embedded rule “should stay liable, even if the rule is wrong”.

On the floor

Industry was already acting on the day’s theme. Visa and Lianlian DigiTech said they had completed a live business purchase in Asia Pacific using a payment credential issued specifically to an authorised AI agent, and launched a business card in Singapore that agents can use within limits the company sets. MYbank, the Ant Group associate, showed an AI agent that took a restaurant owner from request to an approved credit line in about ten minutes, with a human signing off.

Ray Yang, co-founder and chief executive of WasabiCard, told The Fintech Times how quickly attitudes have turned. Three years ago, banking partners in the US and Europe treated stablecoin-funded cards as high risk. In the past year they have come asking for them. He expects stablecoins to disappear into the settlement layer, to the point where “maybe the user does not know that they’re using the stablecoin”. [VIDEO: Ray Yang, WasabiCard]

His constraint is the same one the central bankers described. A card can work anywhere, but it has to be issued somewhere, and regulators care where. WasabiCard uses a local sponsor bank in each market for that reason. To issue cards globally, he said, you need to localise.

In delegates’ hands

The Fintech Times is at the festival in print as well as in person. Our Singapore Fintech Festival 2026 Special Edition is being handed to delegates at Singapore EXPO all week. On the cover is Murtaza Ali, chief executive of JazzCash, on how Pakistan’s largest mobile wallet reached 64 million users, one in three of the country’s adults, and what it will take to become a full-stack Fintech by 2030. The cover story and the full edition are both free to read on thefintechtimes.com.

The festival continues on Thursday, when MAS managing director Chia Der Jiun gives the keynote and the main stage turns to the corridor between Asia and the Middle East.
