title: Stablecoin Issuers Face January Approval Deadline Under GENIUS Act
snippet: Companies issuing payment stablecoins in the United States will generally need regulatory approval to keep issuing them after the GENIUS Act takes effect Jan. 18, 2027. Existing issuers have no automatic grace period, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency said it is still waiting for federal clearance of its application forms before […] The post Stablecoin Issuers Face January Approval Deadline Under GENIUS Act appeared first on PYMNTS.com.
fullText:
Companies issuing payment stablecoins in the United States will generally need regulatory approval to keep issuing them after the GENIUS Act takes effect Jan. 18, 2027. Existing issuers have no automatic grace period, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency said it is still waiting for federal clearance of its application forms before it can accept filings. The agency issued its final implementing rule Oct. 21.

For FinTechs and payments companies, the first step is to determine who actually issues the token, owes customers redemption and is responsible for the reserves, according to an advisory from Anderson Insights. A token marketed under a FinTech’s brand could be issued by a partner. Wallet software, custody or payments integration alone does not make a company an issuer, although these activities can carry separate regulatory obligations.

The law generally covers digital assets designed for payments or settlement whose issuers must redeem them for a fixed monetary amount and represent, or create a reasonable expectation, that they will maintain a stable value, the advisory said. Deposits, including tokenized deposits, are outside that definition. Companies considering a white-label product should review their contracts and operating arrangements to establish which entity assumes the issuer’s obligations.

The OCC will examine who owns and controls the applicant, the experience and integrity of its management, and whether it has the financial resources and controls to carry out its business plan safely, according to the advisory. Applicants should be ready to explain how they will manage liquidity, cybersecurity, operational disruptions and third-party relationships. They should check that reserve arrangements, redemption terms, customer agreements and marketing materials reflect how the product will operate.

Issuers must back outstanding tokens at least one-for-one with eligible assets such as cash, qualifying deposits and specified short-term U.S. Treasury obligations, the advisory said. They must disclose reserve information monthly, have a registered public accounting firm examine it and provide management certifications. Applicable anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations still apply as the OCC and Treasury work on separate rulemaking.

The OCC rule generally requires redemption within two business days once the issuer receives a redemption order and applicable onboarding and other legal conditions are met, according to the advisory. Issuers must notify the agency within 24 hours if requests in a single 24-hour period exceed 10% of the outstanding issuance value of any one brand. They can ask the OCC for more time to redeem. The agency decides whether to grant it.

Eligible existing U.S. issuers with substantially complete applications pending at the OCC by Jan. 18 can request a waiver in writing, the advisory said. The OCC generally expects to grant these issuers relief from the prior-approval requirement absent stronger reasons to deny it. Relief is discretionary and can run for up to 12 months from the effective date. Filing an application or waiver request alone confers no authority to keep issuing. Prospective issuers should plan to secure approval before launch. Existing issuers should prepare their filing materials while the OCC finalizes the submission process. Companies seeking approval from another regulator should confirm that agency’s filing procedures directly. The stakes go beyond a delayed launch. The law provides criminal penalties for knowingly participating in unauthorized issuance.

Exchanges, custodial wallet providers and payments companies should inventory the stablecoins they support and verify who issues them, according to the advisory. A separate provision generally bars covered digital asset service providers from offering or selling payment stablecoins to U.S. customers beginning July 18, 2028, unless the tokens come from permitted issuers or a statutory exception applies. A software-only or self-custodial wallet may fall outside the service-provider definition, depending on its activities.

Providers supporting foreign-issued tokens should check whether the issuer qualifies under the separate U.S. framework, which includes a Treasury determination of regulatory comparability, OCC registration and applicable U.S. liquidity reserve requirements, the advisory said. Companies partnering with an approved issuer should assess their own activities for obligations such as money transmission or custody licensing. These determinations can shape a product’s launch timetable and compliance costs even when a partner handles issuance.

fullText:
Speech by Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive, at TheCityUK National Conference 2026.

  

Speaker: Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive

Event: TheCityUK National Conference 2026, Bristol

Delivered: 19 November 2026

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version.

Reading time: 7 minutes

Highlights

The UK is a global leader in fintech, but we cannot take that position for granted. Firms and regulators alike have to challenge established thinking, embrace uncertainty and try new approaches.

We are changing how we work to keep pace with innovation. That means challenging existing processes, embracing new technology and working with firms to find better ways of doing things.

We encourage firms to come to us early with their ideas. Our Innovation Services are there to help you navigate regulation, test new ideas safely and bring responsible innovation to market.

It’s hard not to feel inspired in a city like Bristol, with its rich history of innovation. 

First, it was aeronautics. Then, it was microchips. Now, it’s fintech. 

Bristol is home to nearly half of all fintech firms in the South West.

Clusters like this one don’t just happen. 

They’re built by people willing to challenge established thinking and take a chance on something new.  

That takes courage.

But for innovation and growth to really thrive, regulators have to be willing to do the same.  

That carries risk. But so does sticking to what we know.  

    

              

How we got here

            						

Our willingness to do things differently in this country has helped make our financial services sector one of the most innovative in the world.

We didn’t get here by accident. 

It took ambitious firms, given the right amount of room to experiment.

The FCA recognised the importance of pushing the boundaries with Project Innovate in 2014.

And the world’s first Regulatory Sandbox in 2016, allowing firms to test innovative ideas with dedicated FCA support.

By 2024, fintech was the most significant job source in UK financial services.

Fintech firms contribute positively to growth, productivity and infrastructure.

No wonder the UK is Europe’s top spot for fintech investment.

But we can’t take that position for granted.

Investment is down. Global competition is up. Funding is getting harder to come by.

And operational disruption is no longer a matter of if, but when.

We’ve recently seen the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange robbed of more than $6 billion.

And a global tech outage that left millions of employees without the tools they need to do their jobs.

Market integrity risks have never been greater.

That's not a reason to hold back on innovation.

If anything, it’s a reason to keep going. We can’t solve these challenges if we stand still. 

But we need to be clear-eyed along the way.

That doesn’t mean certain.

None of us can wait for perfect information.

You decide whether to build, hire or invest before knowing if the idea will work.

We often need to decide whether to act – and how – without the full picture.

Uncertainty comes with the territory.

And in a rapidly changing world, we need to be comfortable making decisions in the face of it.

The decisions that got us here were made that way. The ones ahead will be too. 

          

              

Regulation, growth and innovation  

            						

People often ask how regulation supports growth and innovation.  

But what about regulators?  

Our job is to make sure this sector grows and innovates in ways that create better outcomes for consumers, businesses and the wider economy.  

That means writing rules and working differently: being faster, more accessible, more willing to listen.

And backing experimentation through our Innovation Services, where we help firms navigate regulation and test ideas safely.

We’re seeing results. Firms that enter our Regulatory Sandbox are more likely to raise capital and attract greater investment.

And demand is growing.

We had more applications to the Sandbox and Innovation Pathways in the first half of 2026 than in the whole of 2025 – 92% from firms we haven’t worked with before.

These services are particularly valuable for young firms testing their ideas and business models, with around 70% of applications coming from firms in their first two years.

We’ve scaled and embedded these services across authorisations, policy and supervision. 

Because innovation and regulation are not separate.

          

              

Keeping pace

            						

Markets are changing. So is the speed of innovation.

But so are we. 

Our Innovation Services and the testing they facilitate are faster than sending Q&A between legal and compliance teams, and the regulator.  

And what we learn through experimentation shapes how we regulate and what we share with the market.

You’ve seen this in our approach to artificial intelligence (AI).

Our AI Lab is a place for firms to work with us and explore AI’s potential, risks and opportunities.

It also helps us understand what works.

And today, we’re launching the world-first AI Spotlight Observatory.

Built on cases from over 200 organisations across 150 areas of activity, it shows how firms are really using AI across financial services.  

So you can learn from each other and see where the opportunities lie.

AI could also improve how firms manage risk.

At Mansion House, our chief executive asked whether it’s time to rethink the so-called three lines of defence model: the frontline business, risk and compliance, and internal audit.

I’m taking forward work to explore how innovation could help firms manage risk, grasp opportunities and serve customers better.

That includes better connecting all three lines – with real-time assurance and challenge informed by more timely business insights.

Some firms already use it that way.

Our supervisors are adjusting, too.

As part of being a smarter regulator, we’re modernising how we supervise.

And are looking at whether we ask for duplicative board packs or data that no longer reflects how firms manage risk.

We will also take a step back to understand how firms operate today, and how technology can help us focus on outcomes rather than processes.

Effective risk management is key. 

But it also has to be efficient: timely. Evidenced. Focused on outcomes.

I’ll set out a detailed engagement plan in the coming weeks so we can examine these opportunities together.

Alongside this, our chief operating officer is exploring how to simplify the process around know your customer compliance (KYC).

KYC is an important customer information source, alongside firms’ transaction monitoring, timely investigations of alerts and reporting suspicions.

We know it can feel like the focus is on process over outcomes. 

Now is the time to challenge existing processes and be willing to change what isn’t working. 

If you’re already innovating across your lines of defence or have ideas for simplifying KYC, come and talk to us. 

          

              

Going further 

            						

Our Innovation Services aren’t just for the Next Big Thing. We’re open to any idea that could improve financial services and support growth.

We’re already seeing more firms come forward with ideas.

But we want to hear from firms that haven't used our services much – like those in consumer credit or working on financial inclusion.

That said, not every idea needs our Innovation Services.

Sometimes firms may simply have questions about getting authorised, or the requirements set by various bodies.

That’s why we offer things like our pre-application support service.

And are now letting firms know before authorisation that we’re likely to approve them, helping them secure funding sooner.

We’re committed to working with others to find solutions where a system-wide answer is needed.  

For example, our public statement on safely offering workplace saving schemes, including interactions with our rules and minimum wage requirements.

Our work and our approach reach beyond the UK.

In October, we worked with IOSCO to power its first-ever AI TechSprint, focused on investor education in the age of AI.

Our sandboxes let us test ideas within the existing rules.  

But sometimes the legal framework itself is the barrier. 

Most legislation was written before this kind of technology existed – and it can hold innovation back.

The Digital Securities Sandbox shows what’s possible when rules and legal requirements can be set aside, safely.

It’s a big part of why PISCES, the new private securities market, was up and running so quickly.  

And testing it in the Sandbox means future legislation will be grounded in evidence – not guesswork.

          

              

Take a seat at the table  

            						

There are a lot of conversations happening right now – and there is room for everyone at the table.

So, please, pull up a chair.

We’re making a deliberate effort to get out and hear from stakeholders first-hand.

This year, our executive team alone has made 25 visits across the country.

And we’ve been engaging with consumer groups and firms in Bristol for some time.

Last year, our chief executive met with local fintechs to discuss our strategy and encourage them to use our Innovation Services.

There will be more visits to come.

I know approaching us isn’t always easy.

Too often, firms rule themselves out before they’ve even spoken to us because they don’t have all the answers.

We understand.

But we want to hear from you.

Because while we’re a regulator, we’re also human. And we genuinely want to help.

If you’re innovating, and think your ideas fall within our regulation, come and speak to us.

In return, we’ll listen. Give clear answers. Think differently. And work with others.

Take, for example, agentic AI.

We recently published a joint statement with our partners in the Digital Regulatory Co-operation Forum on protecting people and businesses in an agentic economy.

Because agentic products blur the line between regulated and unregulated activity.

Just because a business describes itself as a technology provider doesn’t mean it can offer financial services without our authorisation.

So, if you're developing or deploying personal agents, come to us early to test your ideas.

We'll move at pace, so responsible innovation can move quickly. 

          

              

Conclusion

            						

The next chapter will be written by those willing to try something new.

Of course, innovation is never without uncertainty. It’s an uncertain world we live in.

Embracing it takes courage – and that’s how we unlock the growth our economy and financial system need.

I doubt those using the Kennet and Avon Canal in the 1800s saw much need for a new way to move people and goods between Bristol and London.

Then came Brunel’s Great Western Railway, which changed everything.

As the most successful entrepreneurs and investors know, sometimes the greatest risk isn’t taking a chance.

It’s standing still.

fullText:
Ant International has connected its global wallet gateway Alipay+ to Pix, Brazil’s popular national instant payment system.

The integration, announced Thursday (Nov. 19), is designed to expand cross-border digital payment access for international travelers.

“Powered by Ant International’s AI-native payment and risk management capabilities, the service allows international travellers using their familiar payment apps to scan Pix QR codes at shops, restaurants, and attractions nationwide, without downloading a new app,” Ant said in a news release.

The launch is part of Alipay+’s larger efforts to promote cross-border digital payment connectivity. Alipay+, helped by its payment partners, connects 150 million merchants with 2.1 billion user accounts around the world. It also works with 16 national QR payment schemes across Asia, Middle East and Latin America, with Pix as the newest addition.

Operated by Brazil’s central bank, Pix has boomed in popularity since its debut in 2020. It is used by more than 22.2 million businesses, according to data from the central bank’s 2025 Integrated Report included in the release.

And as covered here earlier this year, Pix had more than 150 million users as of July, representing around 70% of Brazil’s population, and was processing more transactions than Visa and Mastercard put together.

The PYMNTS Intelligence report “Digital Developments: Charting Digital Payment Growth in Latin America” found that Pix has helped make instant payments into table stakes in Latin America as the service and has become one of Brazil’s most preferred payment methods.

“Since its introduction, Pix has significantly boosted financial inclusion by encouraging the opening of digital accounts across all societal segments and integrating more individuals into the financial ecosystem,” the report said.

The Alipay-Pix partnership follows reports in August that Brazil was interested in linking its payment system to similar offering in other countries.

“Pix is a remarkable example of how payment innovation can transform everyday commerce at scale,” said Weixiao Jiang, Alipay+ general manager for North Asia and the Americas.

“As Brazil welcomes more international visitors, convenient access to local payment services is increasingly important. We’re excited to help connect more international payment apps with Pix, making it easier for visitors to pay while helping local businesses serve more customers from around the world.”

Research by PYMNTS Intelligence has shown the importance of offering consumers access to local payment methods, with 99% of cross-border shoppers saying they expect to pay with their preferred, customary methods. As PYMNTS wrote last year, this emphasizes that “‘all payment is local’ and choice is a decisive factor for consumers.”

title: Checkouts are built for speed. Fraudsters are thankful.
snippet: Faster checkouts may win customers. But as friction drops, are we making fraud easier too?
fullText:
The frictionless conundrum 

The pursuit of higher conversion rates has given fraudsters an ideal playground –– high speed checkouts. 

As physical barriers fade, card-not-present (CNP) fraud rates have surged to 7.5x higher than in-person fraud, with global CNP fraud forecasted to hit $62.9 billion by 2027 according to Visa net data. 

Striving for "zero friction" without real-time back-end verification creates a massive liability. Stripping away user checks may shave off seconds, but it sets the stage for an escalating race to one-click convenience.

The race to one-click everything 

Consumer demand for instant, frictionless purchasing has made manual card entry nearly obsolete, with guest checkout dropping from 44% of e-commerce transactions in 2019 to just 16% by 2025. However, rushing to meet consumer expectations by reducing verification steps can create costly blind spots 

How every second removed from checkout removes another verification point

Stripping friction to accelerate checkout often compromises critical security controls with e-commerce merchants losing 3% of total revenue to fraud annually. To combat these losses, merchants rely on static fraud rules, as manual review remains far too slow for instant purchasing. 

But these rigid controls reject 6% of valid orders out of suspicion — turning away (and frustrating) legitimate buyers. The impact of this can be severe, as 35% of consumers abandon merchants permanently after a single false decline.

Therefore, less checkout verification does not mean less friction; it simply shifts it downstream. The 2026 Global eCommerce Payments and Fraud Report found that over 60% of merchants report rising first-party misuse (AKA friendly fraud), with the average cost to manage and resolve a single dispute surpassing $80. While merchants can shave seconds off checkout, they may pay a far steeper price post-checkout in operational drain, lost inventory and heavy chargeback fees. 

The rise of account takeover and synthetic identity fraud

As front-end verification is reduced, bad actors can exploit these unguarded perimeters at scale. 

Automated botnets now drive widespread credential abuse, impacting 65% of merchants while card testing affects 39% of sellers. Stored merchant accounts have become prime targets for account takeover –– which is the unauthorized hijacking of a customer’s account using stolen credentials. 

Furthermore, millisecond evaluation windows across instant payment rails leave little time for manual intervention, which can accelerate global online scam volume.

Why “frictionless” doesn’t mean “trustless”

To counter this, merchants should shift from visible user hurdles to background data verification — removing the burden from customers and enabling seamless authentication behind the scenes.

By combining real-time cardholder verification and token management to validate account details automatically, security can be embedded across the transaction lifecycle. 

For checkouts that balance speed and security, look for authentication and tokenization tools like: 

Payment Account & Status Validation: Confirms account status, credentials and expiration dates are active before authorization.

Name & Identity Verification (ANI): Matches checkout names with issuer records to prevent synthetic identity fraud.

Address Verification (AVS): Cross-checks billing address data against cardholder records to catch discrepancies.

Card Verification Value (CVV2): Verifies the three-digit code to confirm physical card possession.

Age & Attribute Verifications: Verifies key customer attributes to ensure compliant, secure onboarding.

Unified  Token Vault: Consolidates customer data, card details, and network tokens (Visa, Mastercard, Amex, JCB) into one secure token.

Omnichannel & Alternative Payment Support: Extends tokenization to alternative payment methods like ACH and eChecks, reducing PCI scope and integration complexity.

By validating details and securing credentials in the background, you can flag compromised accounts, boost authorization rates, and deliver a frictionless checkout experience.

The shift to “intelligent friction”

Ultimately, securing modern checkout is not about slowing buyers down but applying security smartly, where it matters most. Rather than trying to eliminate all friction, merchants should focus on "intelligent friction" minimizes friction for genuine customers while adding more checks for higher-risk transactions. 

With risk-based authentication, many merchants can process more valid purchases while saving additional verification steps for high-risk transactions. Alongside fast, automated decisioning, merchants can keep checkouts moving smoothly and more quickly – without exposing themselves to fraud.

fullText:
CheckAlt plans to expand its role across business payments by acquiring Finexio, the company said in a Thursday (Nov. 19) press release emailed to PYMNTS.

The proposed acquisition would add Finexio’s payables technology, supplier enablement and managed payment operations to CheckAlt’s receivables technology and processing expertise, according to the release.

The transaction is subject to customary closing conditions, and CheckAlt and Finexio will continue to operate as separate companies until closing, the release said.

Upon closing, Finexio is expected to operate as Finexio, a CheckAlt company, with CheckAlt President and CEO J. Patrick Law continuing as CheckAlt CEO and leading the combined business, per the release.

Law said in the release that the proposed acquisition will enable the company to deliver a more complete payments offering, help financial institutions and software providers address more of their customers’ payment needs and help businesses simplify how they manage money coming in and going out.

“CheckAlt has been on the move, advancing our technology, strengthening our operations and expanding our reach in business payments,” Law said. “Finexio brings strong payables technology, supplier relationships and operational expertise that take our offering beyond receivables.”

Finexio executes supplier payments through virtual card, ACH and check; manages supplier enrollment, support, exceptions and reconciliation; and offers both AI-powered supplier enablement and hands-on support to establish payment acceptance and support the transition to electronic methods, according to the release.

 Finexio Co-Founder and CEO Chris Wyatt said in the release that the company manages supplier payments from enrollment through delivery and reconciliation.

“Businesses and software providers rely on us to handle that work so their teams don’t have to,” Wyatt said. “Joining CheckAlt would give us the opportunity to bring those capabilities to more organizations and address a broader range of payment needs for our clients and partners.”

The PYMNTS Intelligence report “AI-Driven Accounts Payable: Elevating AP From Cost Center to Strategic Asset,” produced in collaboration with Finexio and published in November 2025, found that artificial intelligence-powered innovation is transforming how companies process invoices, make payments and manage supplier relationships.

CheckAlt announced in June that U.S. Bank clients can now access CheckAlt’s integrated receivables and payment processing solutions through the bank’s online marketplace. This offering enables the bank’s clients to more easily access CheckAlt’s receivables capabilities within the systems they already use, the company said.

title: Klarna launches AI ‘concierge’
snippet: The buy now, pay later provider has waded into agentic commerce with a new tool and aims to expand its longer-term loan portfolio.
fullText:
Dive Brief:

Klarna Group introduced a personal artificial intelligence assistant this week to complement its core consumer lending business, and is debuting it through waitlist invitations, the buy now, pay later company said Tuesday.

“We are bringing AI and agentic commerce to the core of Klarna,” CEO Sebastian Siemiatkowski said Tuesday on a quarterly earnings call with analysts. Klarna users have spent about $34 billion since 2020 using the web browser feature in the existing app, the company said in a press release.

Separately, Klarna said it’s aiming to expand its longer-term installment loans to more U.S. and European consumers. Those loans are Klarna’s fastest-growing and “highest-earning product per dollar of volume,” the company said in its earnings release.

Dive Insight:

Klarna’s AI tool acts as “a personal concierge” for tasks such as booking reservations, drafting email replies, shopping and sending upcoming birthday reminders, the company said in its press release.

The assistant will not complete purchases autonomously – a human is required to authorize payments, a Klarna spokesperson said. Transactions through the AI tool are through a Klarna payment method or a user’s debit card, the spokesperson said. 

The agent interacts via text message and is also available via Meta Platforms’ WhatsApp and Apple’s iMessage text services. The company spokesperson declined to say how many people have been invited to use the assistant so far.

The Klarna tool enters a crowded field of personal AI agents, with consumer offerings that include shopping abilities from Meta’s Muse, Google’s Gemini, Instinct, OpenAI’s dots and Daydream, a New York-based online search and shopping fashion startup. ByteDance, the Beijing-based parent of social media platform TikTok outside the U.S., also plans to release a personal AI agent, Bloomberg News reported last week.

As Klarna bots begin shopping, the company is keen to grow beyond its traditional zero-interest pay later loans. That retail-based lending still accounts for about three-quarters of the company’s gross merchandise volume.

Much of the growth for the lengthier “fair financing” loans has been in the U.S., where the company has partnered with merchants such as Airbnb, Walmart and Southwest Airlines.

Longer-term financing is available at 21% of Klarna’s affiliated merchants, or 283,000, up from about 150,000 a year ago, the company said.

Volume for these loans has more than doubled over the past 12 months, to $12.5 billion, compared to $6 billion in the rest of the world, Klarna said in its earnings report. The company also called out Europe as a region for growth. In the U.S., Klarna’s longer duration loans have terms up to three years and interest rates to a maximum of 35.99%.

For these loans, Klarna targets a transaction margin of 3% to 4% of volume, or “more than three times” what the traditional pay later loans earn, the company said in its earnings report.

For the third quarter, Klarna reported a net loss of $65 million, compared to a $95 million loss in the same period last year. Revenue rose 12% to $1 billion. Active users rose 7% from a year ago, to 122 million in 26 countries.

Klarna also projected a profit for the last three months of 2026, citing “a good start” to the quarter.

The earnings call was expected to be the last for Klarna CFO Niclas Neglen, who is leaving the company at year-end to become the chief financial officer at Adyen, the Amsterdam-based payments processor.

Last week, Klarna announced that Chris Koegel, a vice president at Robinhood Markets, the trading and personal finance platform, will become its new CFO effective Jan. 1.

UK financial watchdogs clarify cyber expectations as attacks rise

              

  

  

  
    

        

    

      

UK’s financial regulators are proposing new guidance to help financial services firms prepare for and recover from cyber incidents as threats grow.

  

            						

The Bank of England’s most recent Systemic Risk Survey cited cyber as one of the risks that would have the greatest impact on the UK financial system. October 2026 saw the second-highest monthly number of cyber incidents reported to the FCA in 5 years, and the highest in the past 18 months, 52% above the previous high recorded in May 2025.

In response, the Bank, FCA and Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) are bringing together existing requirements and lessons from supervisory experience to give firms greater clarity about what is expected of them.

The proposed guidance aligns with recognised cyber frameworks, including the National Cyber Security Centre’s (NCSC) Cyber Assessment Framework. It sets out how firms should manage their cyber risk and resilience without imposing rigid rules, giving firms flexibility in how they meet the expectations in a fast-evolving threat environment.

It covers key areas, including how firms govern, identify, protect against, detect, respond to and recover from cyber risks and incidents. Firms need strong cyber controls to help keep them safe, support well-functioning markets and protect consumers.

Nikhil Rathi, Chief Executive of the FCA, said:  

‘Technology moves fast, and so do cyber threats. The financial sector has a crucial role in tackling those threats, including through products like cyber insurance.

‘Our response shouldn’t always be more rules. Firms have asked us for clarity about what good cyber resilience looks like. This guidance provides it, helping strengthen their resilience, protect clients and the services they rely on.’

Katharine Braddick, CEO of the PRA and Deputy Governor at the Bank of England, said: 

‘Cyber attacks are becoming more frequent, complex and dangerous. Regulators need confidence both that firms have strong cyber controls and that they can detect, contain and recover quickly from incidents. Today’s proposed guidance builds on latest understanding to help firms do that.’

Dr Richard Horne, NCSC Chief Executive Officer, said:

‘We know cyber threats are becoming increasingly frequent and sophisticated, making it more important than ever that organisations can withstand and recover from cyber incidents.

‘The National Cyber Security Centre welcomes this proposed guidance, which will help firms better understand, assess, and strengthen their cyber resilience, in line with our Cyber Assessment Framework.’

Helping firms prepare for AI and quantum risks

Separately, the regulators are publishing additional ‘effective practices’, building on the cyber guidance to help firms practically prepare for specific cyber risks linked to rapid developments in AI and the potential emergence of quantum computing.  

The effective practices include firms tackling vulnerabilities to threat actors using AI, and encourage firms to consider the implications of quantum computing, which could undermine the public-key cryptography that underpins financial transactions.  

These materials reflect the regulators’ position and expertise that allows them to act on the newest risks in the sector, guiding firms through an uncertain and rapidly developing area. 

Notes to editors

The FCA, PRA and the Bank have jointly published a consultation on cyber risk and resilience management.

The consultation closes on 26 February 2027.

Firms, trade associations, technology providers and other interested stakeholders are encouraged to respond. Feedback will inform the final guidance next year.

The proposed guidance is appliable to firms in scope of the regulators' existing operational resilience requirements.  

The approach regulators have taken also reflects the FCA’s focus on smarter, proportionate regulation, providing greater clarity through guidance where new rules are not necessary. This gives firms flexibility in how they meet existing regulatory expectations as cyber risks continue to evolve.

The proposed guidance key foundational cyber risk and resilience areas include:

Embedding cyber risk and resilience in governance and risk management, with clear roles and accountabilities, appropriate board and senior management oversight, defined risk appetite, and regular reporting and assurance.

Identifying and understanding critical IT infrastructure and cyber risk, maintaining up-to-date inventories and maps of critical assets, systems, data and dependencies, and assessing relevant threats, vulnerabilities and potential impacts.

Protecting critical IT infrastructure from cyber threats, applying proportionate controls including secure configuration, vulnerability and patch management, identity and access management, data protection, and controls over third parties and supply chains.

Detecting cyber events and incidents promptly, through effective monitoring and detection capabilities, defined alerting and escalation processes, and regular testing of firms' ability to identify potential attacks.

Responding to and recovering from cyber incidents effectively, with tested response and recovery plans, clear decision-making and communications arrangements, capabilities to contain attacks and restore services, and processes to identify and address lessons learned.

The additional material on AI and quantum computing is not open for formal consultation. However, the regulators are keen to understand from industry whether this type of support is useful and what they would like to see in future.

A recent Bank of England and FCA survey found 88% of respondents expect frontier AI cyber capabilities to have a moderate or high impact on their risk profile over the next 2 years.

In the same survey, 64% said vulnerability management and patching had seen the greatest increase in management attention due to awareness of frontier AI.

title: Act now to be resilient in the quantum future
snippet: Quantum computing will bring significant opportunities to the UK financial sector, but firms need to act now to prepare for a world where a viable hostile quantum computer could break today’s widely used cryptography standards.The financial sector depends on secure information and communication. Cryptography – of which encryption is just one part – helps firms protect their clients’ data, verify who they are dealing with, and maintain trust in their systems.Sufficiently powerful quantum computers pose a real threat to that security. Without trustworthy cryptography, consumers would face fraud, firms would suffer operational disruption, and the integrity of financial transactions and markets would be put at risk.That’s why we are talking to firms about preparing for post-quantum cryptography (PQC) now. Quantum computing will bring significant opportunities to the UK financial sector, but firms need to act now to prepare for a world where a viable hostile quantum computer could break today’s widely used cryptography standards.

The financial sector depends on secure information and communication. Cryptography – of which encryption is just one part – helps firms protect their clients’ data, verify who they are dealing with, and maintain trust in their systems.

Sufficiently powerful quantum computers pose a real threat to that security. Without trustworthy cryptography, consumers would face fraud, firms would suffer operational disruption, and the integrity of financial transactions and markets would be put at risk.

That’s why we are talking to firms about preparing for post-quantum cryptography (PQC) now. We don’t know for certain when a viable quantum computer will emerge, but the coming years will likely see the technology advance at a rapid pace.

Preparing for this new world requires firms to understand where and how they use cryptography and to be able to migrate all hardware and software to PQC, while managing operational risks.

Realistically, for most firms, this will require significant time, investment and effort.

What firms need to do now

So, what kind of timescale are we talking about? The National Centre for Cyber Security (NCSC) recommends 3 key milestones:

By 2028, firms complete a PQC migration plan.

By 2031, firms carry out high-priority migration activities.

By 2035, firms have migrated all systems, services and products to PQC.

Firms should not wait for these milestones before acting and where it is safe to do so, they should seek to be ready sooner. In line with NCSC guidance, we expect firms to act now to: 

Have a thorough and accurate understanding of the cryptography in place across systems and information.

Set clear, achievable, safe and risk-based migration objectives..

Implement migration plans and monitor, test and validate the changes, adjusting them where necessary.

Senior managers should ensure that their firms allocate enough time, investment and resources to manage PQC migration safely and meet the relevant deadlines. Failed change projects accounted for around a fifth of all incidents reported to us in 2025.

How we are supporting firms

We are trialling a new supervisory self-assessment tool with an initial sample of firms and intend to extend it to other firms in due course. This will help firms assess the maturity of their plans and help us understand the industry’s preparedness for PQC migration.

This trial will also help us identify common challenges and examples of good practice, which we intend to share with the sector.

We shared relevant insights from firms in April 2026 and will continue to engage with the industry through our Cyber Coordination Groups (CCGs), the Cross Market Operational Resilience Group (CMORG), and trade bodies and associations.

We will also consult on cyber resilience guidance for firms, including our expectations for how firms should address PQC risks through their cryptographic controls.

title: House Bill Would Put Major Cyber and AI Failures Under Federal Review
snippet: A bipartisan House bill would create a federal board to investigate major cyberattacks, artificial intelligence incidents and technology failures after a nationwide ground stop delayed more than 10,000 flights. The ROOT CAUSE Act, introduced Wednesday (Nov. 18) by Rep. Morgan Luttrell of Texas, with Rep. Ritchie Torres of New York as a cosponsor, would put […] The post House Bill Would Put Major Cyber and AI Failures Under Federal Review appeared first on PYMNTS.com.
fullText:
A bipartisan House bill would create a federal board to investigate major cyberattacks, artificial intelligence incidents and technology failures after a nationwide ground stop delayed more than 10,000 flights.

The ROOT CAUSE Act, introduced Wednesday (Nov. 18) by Rep. Morgan Luttrell of Texas, with Rep. Ritchie Torres of New York as a cosponsor, would put the board inside the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, NextGov/FWC reported Wednesday.

The proposal comes after a midterm campaign in which polling showed widespread concern over AI safety. A September Quinnipiac University survey found that 86% of adults in the United States supported independent safety standards for AI companies. In the weeks before Democrats take control of Congress in January, lawmakers from both parties are pressing for a federal role in investigating critical system failures and addressing the risks posed by AI agents that can act on their own.

The proposed National Cyber and AI Investigations Board would determine what caused significant incidents and recommend ways to prevent a recurrence, the Wednesday report said. Its remit would cover government and private-sector systems, including widely used software and cloud services. The board could examine AI-assisted attacks, harmful actions by agents that exceed their permissions, and outages caused by faulty updates or configuration errors.

This month’s digital disruptions show how that jurisdiction would work. The Federal Aviation Administration imposed a nationwide ground stop Friday (Nov. 13), and a separate Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools. Officials have identified no cyberattack as the cause of either event, according to the Wednesday report.

National security systems, including the classified National Security Agency network whose outage slowed analysts’ work Tuesday (Nov. 17), would be outside the board’s jurisdiction, the report said. The NSA attributed that disruption to maintenance.

The bill would require an act of Congress to abolish, suspend or consolidate the board and bar outside officials from changing or suppressing its findings, according to the report. These protections follow the President Donald Trump administration’s removal of members of the Department of Homeland Security’s Cyber Safety Review Board while it was investigating the Salt Typhoon intrusions into telecommunications networks. The earlier board had faulted Microsoft over security failures that allowed Chinese hackers to access senior U.S. officials’ email.

Rep. Matt Van Epps of Tennessee is proposing separate safeguards for civilian agencies through the AI INSIGHT Act, the report said. CISA would have a year from enactment to establish capabilities to help agencies identify AI agents on their networks, track what they do and restrict their access to what each task requires. Agencies could shut down agents that exceed their authority and revoke access without waiting for vendor approval.

Agencies would also preserve the evidence behind AI-generated findings used in investigations or other official decisions, according to the report. Defense, intelligence and national security systems would be exempt.

The SECURE IT Act, proposed by Rep. Andy Ogles of Tennessee, would codify Homeland Security’s existing role in securing the information technology sector and assign the work to CISA, the report said. The proposal calls for closer coordination with technology providers on testing software fixes, rolling them out in stages and retaining the ability to reverse defective updates. Company participation would remain voluntary.

Sens. Maria Cantwell of Washington and Mike Rounds of South Dakota separately urged the White House to coordinate the use of AI-powered defenses and develop security standards for autonomous agents, according to a Wednesday press release. They pointed to reports that banks struggled to distinguish agents authorized to access customer accounts from unauthorized actors.

Cantwell is in line to chair the Senate Commerce Committee in January, and Rep. Bennie Thompson of Mississippi is positioned to lead House Homeland Security. The leadership change will give Democrats a greater say in how far federal oversight extends, including whether agencies and their vendors should face additional requirements for the AI agents they deploy.

title: OpenAI wallet taps card networks
snippet: The artificial intelligence company has created a digital wallet through which its ChatGPT agent can use Visa, Mastercard and American Express.
fullText:
Artificial intelligence company OpenAI last week launched its inaugural digital wallet for use by its ChatGPT agent, enabling it to make purchases by way of the major card networks.

It’s one of the first instances in the evolving agentic commerce world of an AI agent using Visa, Mastercard or American Express to automatically pay for a transaction based on initial instructions to the AI agent. Mastercard also announced a first-time airfare purchase last week.

The card networks have been working with AI companies to set protocols for agentic commerce, but they’ve all tempered expectations by saying the new bot-driven commerce is in its early stages of development. AI companies and payments providers are racing to set standards for such transactions to help consumers feel comfortable that there will be safeguards when AI agents get their orders wrong, or in cases of fraud.

“We’re introducing ChatGPT Wallet, setting a new bar for secure payments by agents,” OpenAI said in a Friday post. “It’s the first wallet that lets agents pay without access to users’ actual card details and that requires a security check for every purchase, while also preserving existing card rewards and protections for eligible disputes.”

The card networks have also been working with other tech giants to create the agentic technology protocols, but also to set parameters for which companies shoulder responsibility and liability when transactions go awry. 

Google, with its Gemini agent, and Anthropic, with its Claude agent, are also competing in the agentic realm. In addition, digital payments player Stripe has connected its Link digital wallet to Meta’s Muse agent. 

The inaugural ChatGPT wallet transaction was completed using tokenized credentials so the agent is unable to see a cardholders’ card information, such as the security code and expiration date. 

Initially, the wallet feature will only be available to certain ChatGPT users, the OpenAI post said. It will also allow for card rewards and “eligible disputes.” 

Card company executives have suggested AI agents will not be widely used this year, but they have expressed enthusiasm for adding the new channel of commerce.

“Innovation starts slowly until it's sudden,” Visa’s president of value-added services, Andrew Torre, said last week at the KBW Fintech Ecosystem Conference. “What you've seen over the course of the last month, or two months is real interest in agentic commerce.”

“Clients all over the world see this coming and want to get in our agentic sandbox,” Torre said Tuesday at the conference. “There is a lot of consumer interest and, of course, our clients want to be there where their consumers want to be.”

The ChatGPT wallet transaction is the first Amex agentic commerce integration, enabling card holders to engage in agent-facilitated purchases, a spokesperson for that company said by email.

“We're continuing to work with leading AI and commerce partners on additional integrations to bring trusted agentic payments and Amex Membership value into the experiences Card Members are increasingly using,” the Amex spokesperson said.

While ChatGPT’s wallet capabilities are landing just as the U.S. year-end holiday shopping season gets started, executives and analysts don’t expect the new commerce to spool up until next year, at the earliest. 

That’s partly because some significant players involved in digital commerce, including banks and major retailers, are still not ready to participate in AI-based payments. For instance, Amazon and United Airlines have blocked some agentic activity on their websites.

“We should see a lot more agentic commerce happening in 2027 as personal agents become more popular and get more adoption,” Boston Consulting Group Managing Director Inderpreet Batra said in an interview last month.

OpenAI acknowledged in its post that its “early days” for agentic commerce, noting that transactions won’t work if websites block agents or if payment systems don’t recognize agents. 

“We’re starting with limited availability to ChatGPT Pro users, so we can learn from real-world use and work with businesses, banks, and payment networks to improve compatibility and reliability,” the OpenAI post said.

snippet: Walmart+ members visit Walmart’s stores twice as often as nonmembers and its eCommerce site seven times as often. fullText:
Walmart+ members visit Walmart’s stores twice as often as nonmembers and its eCommerce site seven times as often. Now, the retailer is giving those shoppers another way to build a basket through artificial intelligence (AI) agents, management said during the company’s discussion of third quarter results.

Walmart CEO John Furner said Thursday (Nov. 19) during the company’s earnings call that that U.S. use of Sparky, the retailer’s shopping assistant, rose 129% from a year earlier and that baskets associated with its use were 40% larger. Walmart has also announced profiles for shoppers who bring their own agents. Shoppers will be able to set spending limits, track agent purchases separately and revoke access. Approved agents will connect through Walmart’s Agent Gateway.

“Whether customers shop directly with us or through an agent, they should be able to count on accurate pricing, reliable availability, and clear delivery options,” Furner said. In the analyst Q&A, Walmart Chief Growth Officer Seth Dallaire said the company is still learning how conversational prompts change product discovery and how brands get in front of shoppers in those exchanges.

Walmart’s fiscal third-quarter revenue rose 5.2% to $188.8 billion, and global eCommerce sales grew 17%. At Walmart U.S., comparable sales rose 2.9%, with higher unit volume, 1.5% more transactions and a 1.4% increase in the average ticket, excluding fuel. At Sam’s Club U.S., transactions rose 5.1% and the average ticket fell 0.3%, also excluding fuel.

Shares were down 1% in early trading on Thursday.

Grocery sales at Walmart U.S. grew by a mid-single-digit percentage, with pantry items leading food growth. General merchandise sales rose by a low-single-digit percentage, with strength in toys and auto care. The value of general merchandise sold grew at a mid-single-digit rate, CFO John David Rainey said.

Walmart reported market share gains across income tiers, led by upper-income households. Furner told analysts he’d seen pockets of consumer softness earlier in the year. Walmart U.S. ended the quarter with about 7,700 temporary price reductions, down from more than 11,000 at the end of the prior quarter and still above its historical average. For Thanksgiving, Furner said prices were down about 12% on the items that appeared in Walmart’s holiday meal basket in both years.

What Members Are Using

The $120 annual Walmart+ and Sam’s Club Plus bundle launched Oct. 20, shortly before the quarter ended. Dallaire said households that already paid for both memberships were among Walmart’s most frequent shoppers. Dave Guggina, president of Walmart U.S., said early bundle customers were using fast delivery, fuel and streaming benefits and spending more than 80% more online at Walmart than before launch. That’s an early spending comparison, and the holiday quarter will give Walmart a longer period to see how those households shop. Globally, membership fee revenue grew 17% in the third quarter.

Walmart U.S. eCommerce sales rose 23%, and stores fulfilled more than 80% of its online orders. Store-fulfilled deliveries rose more than 40%. Walmart is using that same network to add restaurant delivery, letting shoppers combine a prepared meal with groceries and general merchandise in one delivery.

Walmart raised its full-year constant-currency net sales growth outlook to 4.9% to 5.2%, from 4% to 5%. The fourth-quarter forecast includes a roughly one-percentage-point lift from the shift in timing of Flipkart’s annual sale. The rest of the outlook depends in part on whether Walmart keeps winning a bigger share of shoppers’ spending. Rainey said the revision “assumes underlying sales trends will continue in Q4 with sustained share gains.”

Nonbank installment lender OneMain Financial says it is a step closer to establishing a bank.

The company announced Tuesday (Nov. 17) that the Utah Department of Financial Institutions (UDFI) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) had approved its application to establish OneMain Bank in Utah.

Set to open next year, OneMain Bank will offer things like personal loans, auto finance and credit cards, the company said in a news release.

“For generations, OneMain has focused on understanding our customers’ needs and helping them access responsible financial solutions,” said Doug Shulman, chairman and chief executive of OneMain.

“OneMain Bank marks an important new chapter in our evolution as a financial services company, reflecting the strength of the institution we have built and the trust we have earned over decades of serving our customers.”

OneMain Bank’s deposits will be federally insured, and OneMain Bank will operate independently from OneMain, allowing OneMain to keep its non-bank status. Lee Carter, veteran of companies like UBS Bank and Zions Bank, has been chosen to serve as OneMain Bank’s president, the release added.

title: EPAA Maps Tokenised Money Rules Across 13 APAC Markets
snippet: EPAA launches the Tokenised Money Regulatory Heat Map at SFF 2026, tracking stablecoin and tokenised deposit rules across 13 Asia-Pacific markets. The post EPAA Maps Tokenised Money Rules Across 13 APAC Markets appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
The Emerging Payments Association Asia (EPAA) has launched the Tokenised Money Regulatory Heat Map, a public resource detailing how regulatory authorities across 13 Asia-Pacific markets govern regulated stablecoins and tokenised bank deposits. Developed by EPAA’s Tokenised Money Working Group, the framework debuted during the Singapore FinTech Festival to provide financial institutions, payment providers, and policymakers with a unified view of regional digital asset rules.

While tokenised money is increasingly moving into live commercial use across Asia-Pacific, regulatory frameworks are arriving piecemeal across jurisdictions. According to EPAA’s findings, rules governing the issuance of stablecoins are now in force in four of the 13 tracked markets, yet Japan remains the sole jurisdiction with active rules governing cross-border stablecoin transfers. For banks, payment firms, and issuers planning cross-border products, these regulatory gaps directly shape what can be built and where.

Tracking the Full Lifecycle of Digital Money

Camilla Bullock, CEO at

EPAA

To bring clarity to fragmented supervisory landscapes, the Heat Map evaluates both regulated stablecoins and tokenised bank deposits across six operational stages within each jurisdiction:

Lifecycle Stages: The resource tracks instruments across issuance, reserve backing, custody, domestic payment use, cross-border transfer, and redemption.

Regulatory Status Tiers: Every stage is marked as in place, in consultation, signalling intent, not yet addressed, or prohibited, supported by explanatory notes and primary regulatory sources.

Cross-Border Interoperability: Alongside domestic rulebooks, the map tracks eight cross-border interoperability initiatives—ranging from industry shared ledgers to central bank platforms—and documents how far each has progressed.

“Tokenised money will only work across Asia-Pacific if the rules connect, and most firms are still building that picture market by market,” stated Camilla Bullock, CEO of EPAA. “The Heat Map gives the industry and policymakers one shared view of where each jurisdiction stands at each stage, so the conversation can move to the specific gaps that hold cross-border use back.”

“When clients ask us about tokenised money in Asia-Pacific, the question is rarely whether it’s allowed, but rather, which part of the process is allowed, in which market and when,” noted Antony Ruddenklau, partner, global head of fintech at KPMG International and head of financial services at KPMG in Singapore. “Having that laid out stage by stage, with the sources attached, is the starting point boards and compliance teams need before they commit to a regional plan.”

Bridging Interoperability, Cross-Border Rails, and Par Redemption

Executives across global financial messaging networks, payment platforms, and digital asset infrastructure providers underscored that visibility into cross-border rules and par redemption mechanisms is essential for commercial adoption.

“Cross-border value moves only as smoothly as the least-connected step in the chain,” explained Avalon Ingram, digital assets business lead at Swift. “Seeing regulation mapped stage by stage, next to the interoperability work already under way, shows the industry where common standards will make the biggest difference.”

Matt Kurlanzik, head of government relations for Southeast Asia at PayPal, noted that the resource helps firms building on tokenised money plan regional rollouts with greater certainty:

“Redemption and cross-border use are where products either work for customers or stall,” said Kurlanzik. “A side-by-side view of how each market treats those steps gives industry and regulators a common starting point.”

Highlighting end-user confidence, Kennie Ong, head of solutions for APAC at Ubyx, pointed to the critical role of domestic redemption infrastructure:

“Stablecoins earn trust at the point of redemption,” stated Ong. “If a holder can’t get back to money at par, through a regulated institution in their own market, the earlier stages matter less. The Heat Map makes that step visible market by market and lets everyone learn from each other without having to reinvent the wheel.”

A Living Resource for the APAC Payments Ecosystem

To keep pace with ongoing regulatory developments across the region, EPAA has designed the Heat Map as a continuously updated resource. Users can suggest updates directly through the online portal alongside supporting sources, which are reviewed by EPAA’s Tokenised Money Working Group before changes are published.

Bringing together close to 100 organisations across the payments ecosystem, EPAA continues to drive working groups, policy engagement, and industry forums aimed at developing practical regulatory and operational solutions across the Asia-Pacific region.

The Federal Reserve is also instituting a new access fee that it says will create a more “streamlined experience” for its bank clients.

        

            

        Published Nov. 17, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                The Marriner S. Eccles Federal Reserve Board Building on December 9, 2025 in Washington, DC.

Dive Brief:

The Federal Reserve Board approved a plan to raise prices for some services, including check processing and Fedwire Funds services, by an estimated average 1.4% next year, according to a press release it issued last week.

The central bank also plans to institute a new access fee for some Federal Reserve Financial Services offered by its regional Reserve Banks, according to a Fed staff memo from last month that was attached to the press release. In addition, it will reduce services for paper check processing as it eyes fee increases.

“The Reserve Banks are proposing price changes in 2027 to offset rising costs of providing financial services as well as reduce pricing complexity for customers,” the memo said.

Dive Insight:

The Federal Reserve Banks are required by law to set prices every year that allow them to recover the costs of offering payments and other services to the private sector over the long term, and provide an equity return on those services. The fee increases will begin on Jan. 1, according to the Nov. 12 release.

The 1.4% increase is an average increase across the Reserve Banks’ fee schedule, though prices for the instant payments system service FedNow and for FedACH services won’t be changed other than in keeping with prior plans, the memo said. 

For next year, the new access fee will allow use of various Fed services, with discounts available for some bank clients that meet certain volume thresholds. In tandem with that increase, the Fed said it would reduce some connectivity fees.

“This approach aims to simplify pricing schedules, provide a more streamlined experience for customers using multiple services, and support the Reserve Banks’ cost-recover over the long term,” the memo said.

The Fed is reducing its spending on paper check processing services, eliminating some services for low-volume processing and also reducing its operating hours for handling check processing services, the memo said. 

To fund continued check services while adjusting to lower volumes, the Fed will keep considering ways to reduce services and increase fees.

“These are the first steps in a series of anticipated strategic changes to the Reserve Banks’ Check Services over the coming years,” the memo said.

That follows on President Donald Trump’s effort to reduce U.S. reliance on paper checks, due to their expense versus digital alternatives and vulnerability to fraud.

Overall, the central bank determined that the price increases allow it to keep recovering costs while not undercutting competing private sector offerings. 

“Staff believe that the proposed 2027 changes are reasonable to support long-run cost recovery and do not impact the ability of other service providers to compete effectively with the Reserve Banks in providing similar services,” the Fed’s staff said in the memo.

snippet: If a court rejects final approval of a card-fee settlement over the networks’ swipe fees, the case will go to trial, a federal judge said.
fullText:
A federal judge weighing whether to approve a proposed settlement between merchants and the card networks Visa and Mastercard said the case will go to trial in 2027 if he decides not to give final approval to the accord.

U.S. District Judge Brian Cogan told the parties at the end of a Monday hearing on the proposal that he has not yet decided if he’ll give the settlement final approval. Cogan, who is overseeing the case in Brooklyn, New York, said at the end of the 90-minute hearing that he’ll issue a ruling as soon as possible.

The case pits merchants like convenience retail chain Circle K Stores, owned by Alimentation Couche-Tard, and DoorDash against the two networks, who they allege conspire with large banks to set default interchange rates in violation of U.S. antitrust law. Merchants must pay interchange and other fees whenever a consumer swipes a card to make a payment.

Earlier in the hearing, Cogan told the parties that he won’t do “any more head-banging to get a settlement if I reject this settlement,” which would set up a trial next year. A different judge rejected a prior settlement in June 2024, saying it didn’t treat large and small merchants equitably in some areas of the agreement. 

In June, Cogan granted preliminary approval to the pact, which would conclude 21 years of litigation between a class of 12 million merchants that sued the two largest U.S. card networks and multiple large banks.

About 1,000 larger merchants and trade associations led by the mega retailer Walmart, the National Retail Federation and the National Association of Convenience Stores, have lodged settlement objections that Cogan is considering.

The settlement would trim credit interchange rates by 10 basis points for five years and impose a 1.25% rate for standard consumer cards for eight years. It would also give merchants the right to decline some higher-cost branded Visa and Mastercard premium and commercial credit cards. That would be a departure from the networks’ “honor all cards” rule requiring merchants to accept all cards from the networks if they accept any cards. 

In 2024, merchants paid a 2.35% fee, on average, on card transactions routed over Visa and Mastercard networks, according to industry research organization Nilson Report in 2025. Card swipe fees totaled $198.3 billion last year, with Visa and Mastercard accounting for 60% of those, according to the Merchants Payments Coalition.

Merchants would also gain new rights to add surcharges and offer discounts for cards as a way to steer customers away from cards with higher interchange fees. But large merchants argue that they can’t easily reject the premium cards issued by banks – which offer consumers travel and cashback rewards and carry higher fees – because they are popular with customers.

Cogan’s decision is subject to appeal at the 2nd Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals in New York City.

As part of a brief discussion on litigation risk during the hearing, Cogan said the parties would have about two months to prepare for a trial, followed by a roughly two-month trial. If plaintiffs won, the parties would then offer their views of how the court might craft an injunction, further delaying a conclusion of the litigation, Cogan noted.

A trial process is extensive but “it’s not going to be as protracted as it has been, but still a protracted process, which is one thing I have to consider,” the judge said.

Cogan also oversees a related part of the litigation, a $5.5 billion settlement from the networks eight years ago that covers damages for merchants. To date, the settlement fund has paid about $631.7 million to about 689,000 merchants, according to a report last month from Epiq, the class administrator in the litigation.

title: Researchers spot ACH loopholes
snippet: University of Massachusetts academics have identified vulnerabilities that hackers could exploit in restricted bank accounts.
fullText:
Dive Brief:

Researchers at the University of Massachusetts have published a new study raising the alarm regarding cyberattacks fraudsters can use to target ACH bank transfers, the university said Monday.

The study, titled Credit Without Debit: Formal Verification of Banking Payment Systems, examined three new tactics hackers could have used to pilfer funds from unsuspecting banks and their customers, the university said.

The researchers alerted the at-risk banks to the problem and said the attacks have not been replicable since then. They presented their findings during the ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security on Monday, the university noted.

Dive Insight:

Researchers at the University of Massachusetts contended that hackers could exploit flaws in Nacha’s ACH transfer process. Nacha is the association that oversees the national automated clearing house for payments, setting rules and standards for bank-to-bank transfers.

Though Nacha’s operating rules allow financial institutions to authorize checks once and make provisional credit spendable before the other bank has determined whether to execute the debit transactions, the researchers found that this could result in available funds at one bank while the corresponding debit fails at the other bank. 

“Our goal is to strengthen financial security,” University of Massachusetts Amherst Professor Taqi Raza said in a press release. “The way we strengthen it is we find the loopholes and tell the banks, ‘okay, fix this problem.’”

Raza co-authored the study with Ali Malik, a doctoral candidate in electrical and computer science at the university.

The researchers identified three “credit-without-debit” attacks used by fraudsters and classified them into three threat categories they called: “creditbleed,” “creditmint” and “creditreset.” 

Creditbleed attacks involve initiating an ACH debit to a restricted account at another bank. Then, when the original bank fails to settle the bogus transaction, it will accumulate spendable funds for attackers to spend until the bank with the restricted account eventually reverses the transaction, the researchers said. 

When connecting a new external bank account, banks usually require account holders to enter the correct amount of change used for micro-deposits to verify their ownership. But attackers using the creditmint technique can trick banks into routing small deposits into restricted accounts that can’t send verification deposits back to the original bank, enabling fraudsters to repeatedly trigger those transactions and collect the spoils, the researchers explained in their study. 

In creditreset attacks, hackers use debit-restricted bank accounts to falsely pay credit card payments and increase the card’s credit line. When the card issuer tries to collect funds from the bank, the transaction fails, allowing fraudsters to spend more on a higher credit line, according to the study. 

The university declined to name which banks were affected by these disclosures, because “our work focuses on systematically identifying vulnerabilities in bank-to-bank transfers rather than individual institutions,” Raza said in an email. “The vulnerability disclosure to Nacha [is] handled through the banks; on checking, the reported issues appear to have been addressed in the updated Nacha specification.”

Nacha sees its accredited ACH professionals as mindful of the system’s parameters. They “are well versed in return risk – that an ACH debit can be returned for approximately two banking days for a number of reasons such as insufficient funds or frozen account,” a spokesperson for Nacha said by email. “Whether an originating bank or its ACH originating customer should allow funds from the debit to be withdrawn before the return deadline expires is their own call based on their own business needs and risk tolerances.”

UMass’ study comes as ACH payments have risen in popularity in recent years. In the third quarter, ACH Network payments jumped 5.9% year over year to 9.3 billion, according to an October Nacha press release. The value of those payments surged 10.2% from a year earlier to $25.6 trillion. 

Meanwhile, major payments providers are tracking and bracing themselves for fraud attempts. 

In its analysis of corporate and consumer fraud attacks released in May, Visa said it found roughly $1 billion in scam transactions in the second half of last year. Months later, the company acquired the cybersecurity and fraud-prevention company BioCatch for $2.4 billion to strengthen its anti-fraud offerings.

title: Google wallet returns to Apple
snippet: The wallet app gives Google an early lead among iPhone-wielding agentic shoppers and poses a rival for Stripe’s Link wallet, analysts said.
fullText:
Google’s digital wallet can now be used on Apple’s iPhone and other iOS devices, a strategy change that analysts say signals Google’s enormous ambitions in agentic commerce.

Google announced the new iOS wallet app on Tuesday with a company blog post, 13 years after its wallet’s original and later aborted foray into the Apple ecosystem.  The company’s vice president of consumer payments, P.J. Linarducci, explained in the Tuesday website post how the move will advance the tech giant’s agentic strategy.

“As we look toward the future of shopping, Google Wallet will also be a secure hub for managing agentic purchases across Google,” Linarducci said.

Beyond digitizing loyalty credentials and storing payment cards, the wallet will help Apple users “stay in control of agentic purchases made across Google,” Linarducci wrote.

The wallet doesn’t offer mobile tap payments from Apple devices, but Google couched that unsupported functionality with the phrase “at this time” in its website post.

“This is not a payments play, this is an agentic commerce play,” said Laura Huntley, a managing director with FTI Consulting who advises payment and fintech firms. Huntley noted in an interview Wednesday the significant quantity of technical protocols and other infrastructure Google has built to enable agentic commerce.

Google’s Apple wallet isn’t designed for humans buying things in physical stores, but for agents across the internet, said Yasaswini Pujitha, senior banking and payments analyst at GlobalData, a consulting firm.

“As AI agents take on more of online shopping, the focus of payments is likely to shift from the physical terminal to stored credentials and user controls,” Pujitha said Thursday in an email. “That could position Google well for agent-led payments across both major mobile platforms.” 

Google is positioning its digital wallet for Apple users much as Stripe’s Link wallet is integrated into agentic transactions by Meta Platforms’ Muse personal agent, she said. Last week, OpenAI released a ChatGPT wallet for agentic payments.

In a related blog post Tuesday, a different Google vice president, Josh Woodward, who leads labs, Gemini app and AI Studio operations, articulated how the company sees the Gemini agent completing routine daily tasks, such as grocery orders, scheduling appointments and tracking bills.

Mountain View, California-based Google shuttered the original iOS wallet app about five years after its 2013 debut as the company consolidated its digital payment apps, later folding the Google Pay tool into the wallet for U.S. users in mid-2024.

The wallet app “makes perfect sense because Google has a massive user base and many of them have iPhones,” Shawn Conahan, chief revenue officer at Wildfire Systems, a San Diego-based fintech that sells loyalty and shopping rewards infrastructure, said Wednesday in an email. “Stop thinking of the wallet as just a tap-to-pay vehicle and start thinking of it as a distribution and engagement channel.”

That’s also how Google considers its wallet – an evolution toward a commerce-centered hub that operates as far more than a payment tool, the company’s head of payments, Stavan Parikh, said in an interview last month. He expects the wallet to become the place to manage tasks such as order confirmations, receipts and delivery updates.

“We’re really just kind of scaling the wallet for end-to-end commercial journeys,” he said.

Aaron Press, a research director for data and research firm IDC, who focuses on payments, said that “agentic enablement is a significant factor” in Google’s iOS wallet decision. “Google has been leading the charge in terms of the protocols and processes to enable parts of the agentic commerce ecosystem,” he wrote Wednesday in an email.

However, beyond agent-led shopping, there is “likely a meaningful overlap” of consumers who use Google services and Apple devices, which gives Google the option to capture some online transactions, Press said.

Apple has spent far less building AI infrastructure than many rival tech giants such as Anthropic, Google and Meta, with many analysts viewing it as falling behind in the agentic commerce race. Earlier this year, Apple turned to Google for a partnership in which its Siri agent and other AI efforts are powered by Google’s Gemini. 

The extent to which Google builds agentic commerce functions into the wallet app will be worth watching, “given Apple’s lagging AI efforts relative to Google’s and other megacap tech companies,” including Meta, said Tom Forte, a senior consumer internet analyst at investment bank Maxim Group in New York.

“I would consider this an example of co-opetition to the extent the two companies sometimes collaborate with each other even though they are competitors,” Forte wrote Wednesday in an email.

One reason Google likely declined to add tap payment to the wallet is because of fees that Apple charges for payments made with its devices, Forte said.
